The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now

Sydney Morning Herald August 27, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A great movie never gets old. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Binge right now.

Don’t have Binge? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Disney+.

The stupidity is glorious and unchecked in this Will Ferrell comedy, where he plays a pompous 1970s newsreader who has an identity crisis when he falls in love with Christina Applegate’s capable new co-anchor.

Filmmaker Sean Baker brought his sharp, sardonic feel for the marginalised into the mainstream with this Academy Award best picture winner about a Brooklyn stripper (Mikey Madison) who marries the wayward son of an unimpressed Russian oligarch.

Fantastical, storybook sweet and a plea for kindness, this now beloved Australian family film celebrates an upstart piglet who yearns to do the farm work of a sheepdog. It’s a winning tale, tinged by a smidge of unavoidable reality.

One of the great enduring Hollywood pleasures, this witty, inclusive science-fiction comedy stars Michael J. Fox as the teen who finds himself in the past, upending his parents’ courtship. Inventive, funny and family-friendly.

Starting with co-writer Kristen Wiig, Melissa McCarthy and Rose Byrne, this showcase of comic actresses delivers an unhinged but also insightful exploration of female friendship as preparations for a wedding run amok.

Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci reunited for this real-life mob saga about the Mafia associates – plus a scintillating Sharon Stone – who spin out of control when given the run of Las Vegas. Sumptuous, bloody filmmaking.

In her international breakthrough, Cate Blanchett is a translucent centrepiece who must sacrifice her own desires to survive a murderous 16th-century campaign to reach and retain England’s contested throne. Power is depicted with elegant brutality.

Starring an impossibly young Mel Gibson and Mark Lee as athletic rivals turned World War I comrades, Peter Weir’s compelling war film reveals how the horrors of trench warfare helped form Australia’s national identity.

Ridley Scott updated the swords-and-sandals genre from the 1950s to the age of computer-generated imagery, with a defiant Russell Crowe as the fallen Roman general seeking vengeance on his imperial foes by fighting his way to Colosseum glory.

As much a maximal action invocation as a twisted European fairytale, Joe Wright’s coming-of-age thriller stars a teenage Saoirse Ronan as an avenging innocent sent by her fugitive father (Eric Bana) to kill his CIA adversary (Cate Blanchett).

Still fiercely contentious on both sides, this biographical drama is nonetheless one of Daniel Day Lewis’ defining roles, playing a young Northern Irish man falsely convicted by the British government for a terrorist attack.

Nancy Meyers gracefully aged the romantic comedy into fifty-something abandon, with a masterful Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin as the divorced parents who have an unexpected affair. Steve Martin, and perfect decor, complete the equation.

Greta Gerwig’s resonant, restructured take on an American literary standard, brought to life by an outrageously stacked ensemble cast, is a deeply felt portrait of 19th-century dilemmas and decisions for a quartet of sisters.

An unsettling, intimate psychological thriller for the online age – The Talented Mr Ripley with Instagram – that follows a fan who connects with a rising pop star and becomes an obsessive, and eventually intrusive, member of his entourage.

My pick of Tom Cruise’s blockbuster spy films is the sixth edition, which has a muscular directness from director Christopher McQuarrie and two exceptional foils for the Running Man in Rebecca Ferguson and Henry Cavill.

Emma Thompson wrote and starred in this anarchic, Victoria-era family fantasy, playing the not exactly normal nanny who helps Colin Firth’s hapless widower and his seven unruly children. Great, distinctly British, fun.

On a faltering Californian ranch, a pair of siblings – Keke Palmer and Daniel Kaluuya, terrific together – realise something is not right in the sky, setting off Jordan Peele’s cataclysmic critique of entertainment culture. This one goes places.

A comic genius whose career went to unorthodox places, Jerry Lewis peaked as a technically inventive filmmaker and star with this madcap, big-hearted comedy about a nerdy academic who Dr Jekylls himself into a narcissistic Lothario.

This dexterous crime thriller, directed by Steven Soderbergh, is grown-up entertainment from start to finish as George Clooney and a never better Jennifer Lopez play respectively a bank robber and US Marshal with combustible mutual attraction.

Director John Hughes left high school stories behind for this festive season road trip comedy, where Steve Martin’s uptight executive and John Candy’s garrulous travelling salesman bond through a series of comic misadventures.

A landmark Generation X movie and a delightfully cool celebration of underworld intrigue, Quentin Tarantino’s film does backflips with the narrative structure and showcases an ensemble cast who revel in the juicy dialogue exchanges.

Backed by real-life wife Emily Blunt, The Office cut-up John Krasinski changed lanes and successfully launched a horror franchise with this slow boil post-apocalyptic thriller about a family trying to survive fraught new circumstances.

Opening with a hellacious 25-minute recreation of a historic battle, Steven Spielberg’s World War II epic captures the horror of war and humanity’s debasement. The director’s trademark sentimentality is present but constrained.

One of the all-time great Hollywood comedies, run with whipcrack comic cynicism by Billy Wilder, stars Jack Lemmon and Tony Curtis as 1930s fugitives donning drag to hide out with Marilyn Monroe’s all-female band.

An exhilarating animation that smells like teen spirit, this comic-book adaptation explodes the possibilities of cinema’s favourite web-slinger. The design is immersive, the movement exhilarating.

Rob Reiner mastered every genre he attempted in his crackerjack first decade as a director, including this bittersweet coming-of-age drama, adapted from a Stephen King novella, that boasts deeply felt performances from the teenage leads.

In one of her landmark performances, Cate Blanchett irrevocably reveals every malignant flaw in her privileged classical conductor. Writer/director Todd Field turns a character study into an inexplicable dissection that refuses to simply sum up its subject.

Brian De Palma, a director previously known for Scarface’s excesses, was the surprising right choice to elevate this 1930s crime saga, where Kevin Costner’s FBI agent and Sean Connery’s ornery cop take on Robert De Niro’s Al Capone.

Alfred Hitchcock’s greatest film is a gripping psychological thriller about a tormented private eye (James Stewart) who becomes obsessed with the mysterious woman (Kim Novak) he’s investigating. The visual technique and emotional unease are profoundly intertwined.

A quarter-century on and Ben Stiller’s deliriously absurd comedy, where his nincompoop male supermodel is ensnared in a political conspiracy, remains a rightfully quotable satire rife with ridiculous supporting turns. Take a bow, Owen Wilson.

*Stan is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead.

This transport hub could hold the key to Melbourne’s megacity future

Sydney Morning Herald August 27, 2026

Use the interactive map to see how many more people could live in your suburb by 2101 as we explore the idea of redirecting the booming population to urban transport hubs and regional towns.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Victoria’s population grows by about one person every four minutes and 40 seconds.

Factoring in births, deaths, international and interstate migration, and the fact most of these people will live in Melbourne, Victoria’s capital is well on the way to becoming a megacity of more than 10 million people by 2101.

To put that in perspective, in the lifetime of a baby born today, Melbourne would need to absorb the population of two Perths.

It’s a confronting reality that puts us on a course matching the likes of New York, Moscow and Shanghai, as about 2000 newcomers make Melbourne their home every week.

If Melbourne continues to allow the city’s footprint to expand, Wallan, Whittlesea, Cranbourne South, Sunbury and Eynesbury would see the biggest population boost by 2101.

However, if we focus growth into established areas, some heritage streetscapes in the city’s inner east will be lost and industrial land around our port, in West Melbourne and Port Melbourne, would have to be transformed into residential hubs.

Population and housing projections from Johnny Barnard, founder of the National Forecasting Program at demographic consultancy Informed Decisions (. id), and commissioned by The Age, show the areas of metropolitan Melbourne that would see the biggest population increases. Use the interactive map above to see how your suburb could change.

This week, The Age has explored the dilemma that housing almost 5 million extra residents, in 2 million more dwellings, would create for the city.

In October, The Age and the University of Melbourne will host Melbourne Assembly, a three-day forum bringing together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future.

However we choose to grow Melbourne, a city with a growth rate higher than that of most developed countries, poses challenges for all levels of government and the city’s residents.

Today we ask: Are there alternatives to the way we are handling the growth? Can we do better, and if so, how?

More than seven in 10 Australians live in six state capitals, a phenomenon influenced by the country’s colonial history and the “top-down” establishment of port-dominated settlements that once reported back to imperial London.

European fear of our vast desert interior further marked the coastal capitals as the places to be.

In that sense, the evolution of our cities has been less organic than in many other countries.

Melburnians do not have a direct say in the size and growth of their city.

The federal government is responsible for immigration levels and neither it nor state governments have population policies that dictate how big our cities should be.

Our cities are left to cope with the influx of people as best we can.

While acknowledging the demands and challenges of rapid growth, most planners believe allowing Melburnians to dictate the overall size of the city, would give existing residents too much authority and future residents none.

“It’s not a good idea,” says Pat Fensham, Victorian president of the Planning Institute of Australia, pointing to the experience of New South Wales in 2000.

Then-premier Bob Carr sought to slow the growth of his capital, bemoaning that his government could not keep up with the infrastructure needed to service a booming population. It was a call famously interpreted as Sydney being “full”.

“Carr declared Sydney full soon after the 2000 Olympics and stalled infrastructure investment for a growing city,” says Fensham. “It has taken two decades of freeway and metro line building, et cetera, since he left to get close to catching up and addressing some of the damage done.”

So, if we don’t pull up the drawbridge, what do we do?

Under the “populate or perish” ethos of post-WWII, Australians didn’t stress too much about where all the people would go.

We just kept adding detached single-level housing onto cities that spread into the vast Australian expanse.

But by the 1960s, commentators such as Robin Boyd, author of The Great Australian Ugliness, were scathing of our sprawling suburbs, and politicians such as Gough Whitlam had grown concerned that services and infrastructure were not keeping up with our car-dependent frontiers.

Whitlam’s alternative was to decentralise, proposing the Commonwealth proactively help build and service centres around the country – such as Albury/Wodonga on the Victorian, NSW border – as part of a wider push for regional planning and government.

While Labor’s demise in 1975 put a dampener on decentralisation, the idea is regaining momentum amid growing concern about our capitals as megacities.

“It once seemed far-fetched to decentralise, but it is arguably a better model than the megacity option,” says Dr Elizabeth Taylor, a senior lecturer in urban planning and design at Monash University.

She stresses, however, that revisiting the idea requires big federal commitment, including to the long-elusive dream of fast rail linking eastern coast capitals and regional centres.

Taylor says governments have been reluctant to back decentralisation because it means establishing infrastructure such as train stations ahead of the people who will use them.

“The argument goes around and around in circles, government won’t invest because there’s no accompanying urban plan, but there is no urban plan because there’s no infrastructure.

“To build and nurture real liveable cities, you have to stick at it for 20 or 30 years and well beyond any electoral cycle,” Taylor warns.

Julian Bolleter, director of the Australian Urban Design Research Centre and co-author of Planning for a Continent of Cities, says it seems Australia is at a tipping point where decentralisation may work better than our current sprawling cities approach, and make economic and political sense.

He is encouraging what he calls a national settlement plan, which would redirect population growth away from sprawling capitals and towards satellite cities and regional hubs.

The Albanese government has a low-key National Urban Policy which talks about “a shared vision for sustainable growth in our cities and suburbs” but does not map out a plan of action or spending.

The state government has launched a housing strategy committing to putting 70 per cent of growth in established suburbs, including a network of activity centres.

“But we need more than aspirations. We need to be planning for an Australia of 70 million people,” Bolleter says.

He envisages a “halo of satellite cities” linked by fast trains to Melbourne, an idea that would only work if Melbourne “holds the line on its urban growth boundary”, allowing farms and open space to exist between the city and its satellites – think London and surrounds.

“Not just a line on a map,” says Bolleter. “Something recognisable on the ground – a legible edge.”

Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo and Traralgon, in the Latrobe Valley, are often cited as the obvious candidates to target for more growth, including through faster and more frequent trains.

While many politicians across the spectrum, as well as planners and developers, support the idea of decentralisation, they also doubt it is a realistic alternative for coping with our growth.

Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie, whose electoral office is in Wodonga, evokes Whitlam when she talks of her vision of a network of regional cities with populations in the hundreds of thousands, absorbing half of the nation’s population growth.

She notes how governments of earlier generations planned for the future with transport and infrastructure ahead of population, while “policymakers” now chase their tails with building infrastructure retrospectively.

“We pour people into the major cities, but are creating spaces that are not optimal for humans living in communities,” McKenzie says.

While Fensham is sympathetic to the idea, he says “turning the ship around” to build up regional centres is a big ask.

“To have, say, 50 per cent of growth in the regions requires a massive investment and is not necessarily going to give you the outcomes that you could get by investing in proper transport and other infrastructure in suburban Melbourne,” he says.

Demographer Johnny Barnard has been tracking the development of Australian cities for 30 years. He suggests that rather than thinking about decentralising beyond Melbourne, we should decentralise within it.

“It would be really good if we didn’t think of Melbourne and surrounds as a city, but more as a region, a series of economic rings or spheres of influence.”

Underutilised Geelong would be an important player in that region, says Barnard, and play an important part in spreading the growth load.

Rather than trying to impose a more urban future on regional cities such as Ballarat, Barnard, backs bigger government investment and involvement in key transport hubs, such as Dandenong, Broadmeadows and Melton.

His projections show that these centres already face big growth pressure in the coming decades. The population of Broadmeadows is projected to increase by more than 50 per cent and Dandenong by about 25 per cent by 2101.

Melton already has about 50,000 people and under a “business as usual” growth model will end up with close to 120,000 in the same time frame.

“Assuming we electrify the Melton line, it’s far better to put people around Cobblebank and Rockbank than it is in Armstrong Creek [near Geelong].”

However, Barnard says careful government attention to planning and infrastructure can ensure we build vibrant, liveable centres.

“I would favour decentralisation within the Melbourne urban region; that’s probably more useful, and probably more environmentally desirable.”

As for Traralgon, current Latrobe City Council Mayor Sharon Gibson supports growth “within reason”, while noting the impracticality of a 2½ hour train trip.

“We have a train to Melbourne that actually takes longer than it used to years ago,” she says. “Give us the infrastructure to make it work, so the extra growth does not bottleneck our towns.”

One thing just about everyone agrees on, is that federal and state governments need to be playing a bigger role in ensuring that our cities and towns are well connected, planned and designed to be liveable.

“The very point of living in a city is to be around other people, and the cultural, social and economic opportunities that come with it,” says Taylor. “But we also value the countryside because it’s cleaner and greener. We need both.

“There has to be more to planning than just growth. It should also be about improving the places we live in.”

Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website, including special offers for Age subscribers

Mbappé hat-trick sinks Real Sociedad after Real Madrid jeered by home fans

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 21:39:14 GMT

Kylian Mbappé scored a hat-trick as Real Madrid beat Real Sociedad 4-1 at the Bernabéu on Wednesday ⁠in their first home match since the return of José Mourinho as head coach.

Mbappé put Madrid ahead in the 40th minute before Luka Sucic levelled four minutes later, but the ⁠France forward restored the ⁠hosts’ lead on ​the hour. Vinícius Júnior added a third in the 68th minute before Mbappé completed his treble 10 minutes from time.

It was a winning return ⁠to the Bernabéu for Mourinho, more than 13 years after his previous home match in charge of the club, as Madrid recovered from a disjointed first half ⁠with a ruthless display after the break.

Madrid were jeered before half-time after a sluggish opening in which they ​looked short of rhythm, careless in possession and ‌vulnerable on the counterattack.

“There’s always a sense of justice in the ​boos and the applause, and the odd boo now ‌and then doesn’t do anyone any ‌harm – it helps you grow,” Mourinho said at full time. “We all know the Santiago Bernabéu and just how demanding the fans ‌are here, and I’m very pleased with how my players responded under pressure and put in a great second half, in which we could even have scored more goals.”

Real Sociedad carried ‌the sharper threat early on and almost went ahead in the 10th minute when Takefusa Kubo intercepted ‌a loose pass near the edge of the box and slipped in Mikel Oyarzabal, whose close-range effort was kept out by Thibaut Courtois.

Fenerbahce upset Lyon in the Champions League playoffs on Wednesday to advance, while Viking Stavanger joined fellow Norwegians Bodø/Glimt in the league phase with victory over Dinamo Zagreb.

With the teams locked at 1-1 from the first leg in Istanbul a week ago, the Turkish giants opened up a 2-0 lead in the first half of the return fixture in France. Vedat Muriqi and English defender Archie Brown [pictured] were on target for the visitors, with winger Malick Fofana giving Lyon faint hope in the second half.

Viking hit back from a goal down on the night against Dinamo Zagreb, winning 3-1 in Norway and 5-3 on aggregate. Albania's Arber Hoxha gave Dinamo an early lead but Zlatko Tripic equalised from the penalty spot just eight minutes later. Two early goals in the second half from Edvin Austbø and Tobias Moi sealed Viking’s progress to their first Champions League group phase.

Barnabas Varga scored a double and former Real Madrid forward Luka Jovic added another as AEK Athens cruised into the league phase with a 4-0 thrashing of Levski Sofia. Romania's Razvan Marin added a penalty as the Greeks booked their progress following a 0-0 draw in the first leg in Bulgaria.

Panama’s Cristian Martínez scored the extra-time winner for Slovan Bratislava as they overcame Slovenian champions Celje. After a 1-1 draw in the first leg, Andraz Sporar gave the Slovakians an early lead at Celje but Svit Seslar equalised fom the penalty spot, before Martínez secured a 3-2 aggregate success. AFP

Champions League: qualified teams and predicted pots

Pot 1: Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Liverpool, Internazionale, Manchester City, Arsenal, Barcelona, Atlético Madrid.

Pot 2: Dortmund, Roma, Sporting CP, Aston Villa, Porto, Manchester United, Club Brugge, Real Betis, PSV Eindhoven.

Pot 3: Feyenoord, Lille, Bodø/Glimt, Napoli, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Fenerbahce, Shakhtar Donetsk, Galatasaray.

Pot 4: Slavia Prague, Slovan Bratislava, Stuttgart, AEK Athens, Lask, Como, Lens, Viking, Sabah.

The visitors went close again in the 34th minute, Sergio Gómez flashing a fine volley just wide of the far post, as the Bernabéu crowd began to voice its frustration.

Mbappé briefly changed the mood five minutes before half-time with a flash of class. Fede Valverde collected ‌the ball just beyond midfield and split the defence with a superb pass, allowing Mbappé to surge into the box, cut left and lash a shot into the top ​corner.

But Madrid’s defensive uncertainty returned four minutes later. Ibrahima Konaté, Dean Huijsen and Álvaro Carreras were all caught out after Job Ochieng latched on to a long ball, his deflected effort falling to Sucic on the right, who had time to steady himself and drill a low shot past Courtois.

Mourinho sent on Marc Cucurella at ⁠half-time and Madrid emerged transformed, with Vinícius and Mbappé stretching the visitors ​with direct running and greater intensity.

The ​hosts regained the lead on the ​hour when Mbappé and Jude Bellingham exchanged a sharp one-two, leaving the France captain ​free inside the box to ‌beat Álex Remiro ​with a low finish. Eight ​minutes later, Bellingham’s pressing won the ball back near the byline and his low cross gave Vinícius the simplest of tap-ins from close range.

Mbappé completed the win in the 80th minute after Vinícius slipped a clever pass behind the defence, the forward lifting a composed chip over Remiro to seal his hat-trick.

“This guy is incredible,” Mourinho said of Mbappé. “I see him really hungry to make history with Real Madrid, and I see a team where, despite Kylian being Kylian, it’s hard for me not to talk about the team.”

How the Meta settlement may change social media forever

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 21:32:54 GMT

Instagram and Facebook’s parent company agreed to sweeping alterations and a payment of upto $18bn to settle a landmark trial

Meta’s agreement to change how teenagers use its social networks marks a major turning point for the US tech giant, setting a precedent that could significantly reshape how other social media operates in the coming years.

Meta agreed to substantial alterations to Instagram and Facebook on Wednesday as part of a settlement to end a landmark lawsuit. Dozens of US states had accused it of addicting and harming children with dangerous products. The company also agreed to pay up to a combined $18bn over a decade to several US states and territories involved in the suit.

The changes may be powerful enough to alter teens’ behavior and curb social media’s worst ills, they may not, but the attorney generals did what the US Congress never has: compel a social media company to change its operations to protect children.

Forcing Meta to rework how its social networks operate by default on a level that parents and children will notice is a major concession by the company. It is the first time in the US that Meta has been forced to change key features of the experience of its social networks’ everyday users.

Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, whose ages the company will be obligated to verify. That includes a daily usage limit of two hours, blocking social media use at night, disabling notifications during school hours and a ban on displaying “likes”.

The new safety features will be turned on by default, a powerful tweak and a change from Meta’s previous opt-in approach to teenage safety and parental control. The settlement repeats again and again the word “default” when describing injunctive measures.

The amount of money is the highest-ever financial payment by a tech firm in the US, but does not pose significant threats to Meta’s business. The attorneys general had originally estimated damages of around $200bn, equal to the company’s entire revenue in 2025. Meta’s own yearly spending dwarfs the settlement amount. It has told investors that it will make investments in AI worth at least $130bn this year.

Financial damages weren’t the states’ primary objective in this suit. Instead, it was consequential changes to the way Meta’s platforms operate.

“This is a down payment, if you will, on protecting our kids,” Rob Bonta, the attorney general for the state of California, said in a press conference on Wednesday. “It is transformative. It is a watershed moment. It is a milestone mark.”

For its part, Meta’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the company was “pleased to announce” the agreement.

The changes build on others Meta has introduced in recent years in response to concern over young people’s wellbeing, including the introduction of dedicated teen accounts in 2024, a new product the company touted at trial. The attorneys general filed their suit against the company the year prior, and Meta may have debuted Teen Accounts to avert disaster in court.

Bonta said during the press conference that Meta’s prior teen safety tools were essentially ineffective.

“They seem to be performative and superficial and pretextual in response to our litigation,” Bonta said. “They were essentially safeguards that were easily overridden by a child’s own swipe of the finger.”

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

In the settlement agreement, the attorneys general pushed the company to do more.

In a binary viewing, the settlement is a victory for the states. How much of a win it is will be determined by history, but in the present, the attorneys general achieved their aim, forcing the company to take measures to protect young people in the US.

The company is putting the agreement forward as a precedent for other social media companies to follow. Faced with new handicaps, it is cajoling competitors such as TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same measures.

“This framework will only work if all our peers join us,” Meta’s Mahoney said. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution.”

It might not have to do much convincing. Bonta indicated in a press conference that he and other states’ lawyers were in talks with other social media companies about also making changes.

“Mostly what needs to be done is getting similar protections across the industry with TikTok, with YouTube, with Snap,” Bonta said. But, he added, “Meta is a major player.”

Plug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first time

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 21:30:23 GMT

DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity

Plug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity.

Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers.

Argos will be the first to offer the DIY solar systems this week, helping people living in flats or rented homes without roof access to lower their bills by generating their own electricity.

The rival retailers Amazon, Currys, B&Q and Screwfix are also expected to stock their shelves with plug-in panels within the coming weeks at prices starting from about £400 to £500 depending on the capacity of the system.

The devices are already popular in Spain and Germany, where they are known as Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant) because they can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.

The solar power flows directly into the property’s electrical circuit to power appliances without needing to buy as much from the grid. Each solar system must be registered so Great Britain’s National Energy System Operator can gauge how the cumulative impact of these panels could cut the need for gas-fired power or imports.

In the UK the 800-watt solar systems due to go on sale will be about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar set-up, meaning they are unable to provide enough energy to power a home but they could save the average household up to £110 a year on their annual electricity bill.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Plug-in solar is a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills and start saving straight away.”

Graham Biggart, the managing director for Argos, said: “By making this technology more accessible, we’re putting more power in the hands of our customers and helping them explore practical ways to manage energy use at home.”

The savings possible from each solar system will depend on how much solar power is generated, which could be affected by the orientation of each solar panel and the weather on any given day.

“There are also important safety considerations, particularly around the suitability of older electrical systems, the safe mounting of panels and the potential for people to use products or equipment incorrectly.”

Joanna O’Loan, a manager at Energy Saving Trust, said: “While the savings will vary from home to home, plug-in solar panels will give more people greater control over their energy use and costs. ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 21:30:23 GMT

Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way

Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme.

He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months.

Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting.

“It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.”

A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years.

But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated.

“I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people. The last thing we want to see is a diagnosis of problems leading to a life on benefits.”

At a roundtable discussion, McFadden asked each of the young people how they felt as a result of their move into paid work. They cited better social lives and clearer daily routines.

“I’m so conscious, having done this job for almost exactly a year now, that belief and confidence is a big part of the picture,” McFadden told journalists afterwards. “We mustn’t blame young people for the challenges they are facing in the labour market.”

The number of Neets in the UK recently topped 1 million – with the latest data due out on Thursday.

Alan Milburn, the Blair-era cabinet minister reviewing youth inactivity for the government, has warned that the number could hit 1.25m by 2030, without intervention. His final report is due in the autumn.

McFadden made clear that welfare reform would probably be part of the government’s response, criticising the “black and white” distinction in the current universal credit system.

“There’s a design flaw in the universal credit system, which too readily separates people into ‘fit for work’ and ‘unfit for work’, and when they are unfit for work, leaves them without any support or any conditions,” he said. “That’s what I call the culture of ‘signed off and written off’. I think we need to change that.”

He highlighted a recent initiative under which claimants with no obligation to look for work have been asked to attend voluntary interviews with work coaches at their local Jobcentre.

McFadden had started the day at a branch of Sainsbury’s in London, stacking shelves in the bread aisle, alongside the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan.

The trio were highlighting the fact that Sainsbury’s is offering 10,000 internships for young people.

McFadden praised Boots and Sainsbury’s, and encouraged other big employers to play their part in what he called the “national cause” of tackling youth unemployment.

Asked whether it was a good use of public money to be subsidising corporations to take on young people, he said: “I’m enthused when businesses like Boots or Sainsbury’s – or any business in the country – steps up and says: ‘I want to play my part here.’ And if there’s a bit of a financial incentive in it, that’s fine.”

The jobs guarantee scheme will eventually be available to 18- to 24-year-olds in Great Britain who have been claiming universal credit and seeking work for at least 18 months, with the aim of creating 90,000 subsidised placements over the next three years.

It is initially being piloted in six areas with high unemployment, including central and east Scotland, Birmingham and Solihull, and south-east and south-west Wales. The government intends it to be nationwide by November.

The Murder Detective review – is justice for Lyra McKee really this impossible?

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 21:00:22 GMT

It’s painful to see Northern Irish police bang their heads against the wall as they hunt for the journalist’s killer. But there are still important moments here – including remarkable footage from an MTV show that never aired

The killing of Lyra McKee, a journalist shot while observing a riot in the Creggan area of Derry, Northern Ireland, on 18 April 2019, is a case that remains officially unsolved. Last month, three men were found not guilty of her murder after a two-year trial; so far, there has been only one conviction, for possessing the gun that killed her.

That a member of the republican paramilitary group the New IRA fired the weapon is not in question. Many of the approximately 150 people who were standing within metres of him at the time must know who he is. But this is a part of Northern Ireland where police work is still, more than 25 years since the Good Friday agreement, met with violent intimidation or resolute silence. The extinguishing of McKee’s bright, hopeful talent is a story destined not to end in relief or resolution.

The challenge faced by the film-maker James W Newton, in his three-part documentary on the investigation into McKee’s death, is to turn an agonisingly unsatisfactory situation into satisfying journalism. He struggles. The programme is made with care and skill, but it is a bleak situation in which not much can happen and few insightful things can be said.

As the title indicates, The Murder Detective is not chiefly about McKee. Instead, having been granted unprecedented behind-the-scenes access to a terror-related murder investigation by the Police Service of Northern Ireland, it concentrates on Jason Murphy, the detective hunting for the killer. We see raids on the houses of suspected New IRA members and hushed meetings with MI5 agents whose identities are concealed, but Murphy’s work is based almost entirely on one type of evidence: CCTV footage of the crime.

This gives The Murder Detective its startling opening scene. To the sound of increasingly panicked chat on police radios, a line of armoured vehicles is surrounded, then pelted with petrol bombs; a stolen truck is driven up to the junction in front of the police vans and torched. Then a figure in a hoodie, a mask and striped Adidas tracksuit bottoms starts firing a pistol.

As Murphy and his team pore over the pictures frame by frame, they spot a documentary camera operator in the background of one shot, which leads them to the case’s strangest quirk: there is more footage out there. Much more, in fact, because, when the riot began, the TV presenter Reggie Yates was there, making a documentary for MTV about Saoradh, the political wing of the New IRA. Murphy commandeers the tapes.

The Yates film is by far the most remarkable part of The Murder Detective. Yates is in the cars and houses of people Murphy suspects have close links to the New IRA’s leaders, looking over their shoulders as their phones flash up Facebook notifications reporting that the police are in the vicinity and something is about to go down. As he walks through the crackling Derry night with these forceful young men, the sense that Yates has lost control of his project becomes overwhelming. Eventually, after being told by a local person that the riot may be taking place only because he is there, Yates withdraws; he is not present when the shots are fired.

Questionable as Yates’s actions may be, it’s noticeable that the rest of The Murder Detective lacks a scoop to match the MTV documentary (which has not been aired). Newton attempts to give us a backstory for Murphy, but finds nothing unusual to explain what drives him psychologically. The programme can’t decide whether this is Murphy’s show or not; he never emerges as an engaging protagonist. As for the investigation, Murphy and his team arrest and interview people whom they believe to be increasingly senior members of the New IRA. But since all of them refuse to say anything, each interrogation is less compelling than the last.

Having embedded itself with the cops, The Murder Detective seems to feel obliged to give them extensive screen time, an investment the police never repay. More memorable are the scenes with McKee’s grieving family – particularly her raging and focused sister Nichola – but her work as a journalist is only briefly explored. Perhaps it was not considered to be relevant, as it seems McKee wasn’t targeted deliberately – she was standing near the police when they were shot at – but it would have been valuable context, since McKee wrote about how, in a supposedly peaceful post-Troubles Northern Ireland, young men have been left behind, making them vulnerable to becoming the victims or perpetrators of violence.

The Murder Detective mentions that the New IRA hides behind a small army of young male recruits, but it doesn’t analyse the socioeconomic factors that enable it to do so. Instead, it watches the police bang their heads against the same wall, over and over. Justice for McKee remains tragically elusive.

The Murder Detective is on Channel 4

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 20:58:36 GMT

A new season at the snazziest modern stadium in England and something extremely welcome for Tottenham. A home win over domestic opposition. There were only four of them last season; three in the Premier League with the final one – over Everton on the last day – helping them to avoid relegation. Had they lost that, this Carabao Cup fixture against Charlton would also have been played in the Championship.

Spurs needed this tonic for another reason – to begin the clean-up operation after Saturday’s awful 3-0 defeat at Brentford. The season could not have started any worse. With no European football, a decent cup run or runs are imperative and Spurs got themselves up and running in this competition on a night when everything came together perfectly.

For a good while, it looked as though Mikey Moore was going to be the headline act. The homegrown 19-year-old broke the deadlock with a vicious drive from the edge of the area; it was the purity of the strike that made it. But then came Sávio.

Spurs were 3-0 up with further goals from Dominic Solanke and the substitute, Kevin Danso, when Roberto Di Zerbi sent on his £75m signing from Manchester City for his debut. It would be a devastating cameo from Sávio, something to wet the whistle for bigger challenges ahead.

It took him just 11 minutes to score and it was a lovely goal – a glide inside from the right and a fizzing low shot into the near corner. There was more. Sávio once again showcased his skills when slicing inside, putting one Charlton defender down with a feint and getting away from another. The shot hit his teammate, Ben Davies, and went in.

Charlton would have the last word when another substitute, Lloyd Jones, headed home from a corner. They deserved a goal. The major takeaway was the sense of possibility brought by Sávio.

De Zerbi has been honest about how his team have not been ready to start the Premier League season – a result of injuries, players returning late from the World Cup and a pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia that was sub-optimal, to say the least. The sense with his selection was of the calvary returning.

The manager started Destiny Udogie, Rodrigo Bentancur, Mateus Fernandes and Solanke, players that were fit enough only for the bench at Brentford. Pedro Porro and Micky van de Ven, who did not kick a ball in pre-season and were not available to face Brentford, were among the substitutes. There was no Marcos Senesi or Sandro Tonali in the squad.

De Zerbi’s idea was not to take chances. Whereas his Charlton counterpart, Nathan Jones, seemed to see it as a free hit. He made 10 changes to the team that he sent out for Saturday’s win at West Ham, which made it two Championship victories out of two for the season. Preston at home on Saturday was the priority.

The 6,000 travelling Charlton fans were determined to make themselves heard – even more so after their team lost both of their centre-halves, Collins Sichenje and Billy Koumetio, to injuries in the 15th minute. Sichenje was taken off on a stretcher in obvious distress.

Spurs were always going to dominate the ball. The question concerned what they could create with it. The answer at the outset was very little. De Zerbi’s starting shape was 4-3-3, Bentancur in the No 6 role flanked by Lucas Bergvall and Fernandes. Spurs did not threaten until the 30th minute when Solanke had a shot blocked and Archie Gray extended the goalkeeper, Tiernan Brooks, with a low prod on the rebound.

Charlton might have been in front by then. Greg Docherty exploded a drive through a crowd that Antonin Kinsky did well to save, and Nathan Asiimwe headed narrowly off target.

Spurs upped the tempo after the Brooks save from Gray. Fernandes was good. There was a flicker from Mikey Moore, even if the end product was not there. Then it was. Gloriously. When Moore moved inside from the right, the Charlton player close to him – Millenic Alli – slipped. Moore knew what he had to do and the sweetness of the left-footed connection took the breath. The shot ripped through the hands of Brooks. The power was too much.

Meta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram as it settles US trial over teen addiction for up to $18bn

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 20:30:49 GMT

US tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on nighttime use

Meta agreed to significant changes to its Instagram and Facebook apps in a settlement that ended a landmark lawsuit on Wednesday. Dozens of US states had accused the tech giant of addicting and harming children with dangerous products.

The agreement curtails a major trial in California and will require the social media company to pay up to $18bn. Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and blocks on nighttime use nationwide in the US.

This is the first time in the US that Meta has been forced to change key features of the experience of everyday users.

The jury trial, which took place in federal court in Oakland, California, began with opening statements just last week. California and 28 other US states sued the $1.36tn (£1tn) company over allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claimed the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. As part of the settlement, the company denies wrongdoing.

“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families,” Rob Bonta, the attorney general for California, said in a statement. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms – and will do it within months.”

Bonta said those changes included time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters and more.

The $18bn settlement will be divided between the states over a period of 10 years, subject to court approval. For example, California would receive between $1.5bn and $2.1bn and Colorado will get about $615m.

“The relief we are getting in this settlement is very meaningful and well beyond what any court has ordered or is likely to order,” said Phil Weiser, the attorney general for Colorado, adding: “The focus of this case was to protect our kids.”

Throughout the proceedings, Meta denied all allegations saying states are chasing an “outlandish payout”. On Wednesday, the company’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the settlement reached with the states would only work if all social media companies changed their platform designs.

“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok, Snap, and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Mahoney said in a statement. “As a parent, I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically, and of this new groundbreaking agreement. But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta’s lead.”

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap face thousands more similar US lawsuits brought by families, individuals, school districts and other attorneys general. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February, being ordered to pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.) Two more lawsuits that were slated to go to trial this summer, one federal and one in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.

Meta lost a separate suit, brought by the attorney general of New Mexico, where it was ordered to pay nearly $1bn to the state of New Mexico for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms.

The trial in Oakland was expected to last for several weeks with dozens of witnesses taking the stand. Instead, there were only four days of proceedings.

Jurors first heard from the states’ star witness, Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower. He testified that the company had a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms.

Béjar said that Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, was aware of the harms of Instagram and Facebook, but that the executive publicly touted the platforms’ safety.

“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar testified.

Zuckerberg had been listed as a witness in the trial but did not testify before the settlement agreement was reached.

On Tuesday, questioning of Adam Mosseri, the Instagram CEO, began with the lawyer for the states accusing the company of touting safety features for teens, but not being forthcoming that young people don’t use them.

When the executive was faced with multiple questions about not disclosing those low user numbers, Mosseri brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”

Derbyshire police confirmed on Monday that Carse had briefly been detained on suspicion of “being drunk and disorderly” before being “de-arrested”, but the Guardian has been told that their investigation remains live.

In a subsequent statement released on Wednesday, first reported by the Telegraph, Derbyshire police confirmed they are investigating allegations of assault. “We are investigating allegations of assault in Derby city centre,” the statement read. “No arrests have yet been made and the investigation is ongoing.”

It is unclear at this stage whether Carse had any involvement in the alleged assault, but the revelation that the arrest may have involved more than a row over a spilled drink will intensify the spotlight further on England’s cricketers following a torrid few months dominated by headlines involving late-night misbehaviour.

Eight England players including Stokes and the white-ball captain Harry Brook have been involved in alcohol-related incidents since last November, with the returning Test captain, Joe Root, admitting on Tuesday that he was “hacked off” by Carse’s arrest just days after he announced he was lifting a midnight curfew that had been imposed by management on England’s players because he believes they should be treated as adults.

As previously reported by the Guardian, the phone footage of Carse was filmed after he was denied re‑entry to the bar shortly before closing time at around 4am on Sunday morning.

The 31-year-old had left the building following “an exchange of words” with a member of the public who spilled a drink on him.

The England and Wales Cricket Board announced on Monday that Carse would not be available to face Pakistan this week, after he was released from the squad from last week’s first Test victory at Headingley, which led to him playing for Durham against Derbyshire.

Carse will remain unavailable for England pending the outcome of an inquiry by the Cricket Regulator, but with the police still investigating that process has yet to begin so he could face a lengthy exile. He has been selected by Durham for Thursday’s home County Championship match with Gloucestershire.

Andy Burnham has dropped his support for capping political donations, causing anger among activists and Labour MPs who have long campaigned for change to the way parties are funded.

The prime minister has decided not to back amendments to the elections bill, which would cap the amount a person or an organisation can give in a single donation, according to government sources.

The decision comes after a lobbying campaign from Labour’s trade union backers, who said amendments to the bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages next week, could undermine their ability to donate to the party. It is also a retreat from the support Burnham gave to the idea just a few weeks ago, when he emailed a campaigner for electoral reform to say he would support a donations cap of £500,000.

Stella Creasy, one of the Labour backbenchers who has tabled an amendment calling for a donations cap, said: “Millionaires are increasingly treating British politics as their plaything – splashing the cash to get the outcome they want and the next election as their cup final.

“The public won’t forgive us if we miss this chance to clean up Westminster because we are squabbling with each other.”

Shaun Bowler, the campaigner to whom Burnham promised his support in May, said: “Andy Burnham promised me a proper cap on political donations and a ‘wholesale culture change’ in Westminster. If his government now refuses to back a donations cap, then he has broken the promise he made to me – and to voters.

“I wanted to believe the positive message he gave me. I wanted to believe that someone was finally going to take on the culture that has left so many people feeling that their voices don’t matter and that wealthy people can buy influence over our government.

“But words mean nothing if they disappear the moment power is won. Large political donations are not democratic. They create influence, whether politicians want to admit it or not. The prime minister has one chance to start rebuilding trust: the representation of the people act.

“He told me he wanted change. Now he needs to keep his promise and act.”

Darren Hughes, the chief executive of the Electoral Reform Society, said: “Huge donations have a corrosive effect on trust in politics as they leave the public wondering what donors expect in return for their money.

“A donations cap is a crucial step to ending the impression that our politics is for sale to the highest bidder and rebuilding that trust, which is currently at record lows.”

However, a Labour source said: “The representation of the people [elections] bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising.”

The elections bill, which returns to the Commons next week, is one of the most hotly contested of Burnham’s first few months in office. The bill was intended to lower the voting age to 16 and limit donations by foreign donors, but many in the Labour party believe it should go further in a number of areas.

Rushanara Ali, the Labour MP who helped write the bill when she was a minister in the communities department, recently told the Guardian that she felt it was too “timid” and “incremental”, and urged Burnham to strengthen it with amendments.

Some Labour MPs intend to use the next stage of the bill to try to introduce clauses banning cryptocurrency donations and cracking down on social media misinformation at election times.

Others want Burnham to back their idea of a national commission on changing the voting system – something the former Greater Manchester mayor has repeatedly backed in the past.

The government has already said it intends to cap donations by British people living abroad at £100,000, but a big fight is now brewing over whether to apply a similar cap to domestic donations.

In May, Burnham signalled he would back a £500,000 cap, telling Bowler over email that he thought a donations cap “would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.

He added: “As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”

Once Burnham got into office however, some of Britain’s biggest trade unions mounted a campaign against the idea, urging MPs not to back an amendment by Creasy to cap donations at £100,000 or another by her backbench colleague Alex Sobel to set the bar at £1m.

Last month, GMB wrote to 80 MPs who are members of the union warning: “We believe this amendment risks having significant unintended consequences. Trade unions are already subject to a level of statutory regulation over political expenditure that no other membership organisations face.”

Creasy is now changing her amendment in a move to placate union worries, proposing a £500,000 cap that would be gradually reduced until ministers intervene to set it at a level with which they feel comfortable.

She said: “Our new amendment would give British democracy the breathing space to get a donations cap right.”

However, even this compromise does not appear to have done enough to win ministerial support, which is likely to be crucial for securing enough votes to pass.

Those close to the process say capping donations is not a priority for Burnham and not a subject over which it would be worth triggering a fight with Labour’s biggest backers.

OpenAI staff observed warning signs before AI agent hacking crusade caused global alarm

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 19:00:20 GMT

Firm says ‘early signals … could have triggered an earlier response’ as it releases report into Hugging Face hack

OpenAI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its leading-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped their training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm.

The San Francisco AI company conceded on Wednesday that “early signals … could have triggered an earlier response”, as it released a report into the days-long July hack of a major software repository, Hugging Face, considered the first autonomous agent cyber-attack.

As fresh details emerged about how “the collective” – a squad of about 700 autonomous agents – launched their campaign, celebrating their hacking breakthroughs with exclamations such as BOOM! and Whoa!, OpenAI said that in late May an internal team observed that one of its AI agents undergoing internal testing was using a message board that AIs had unexpectedly improvised to share information. It also said that the team observed “instances of disallowed internet access” and that a week before the Hugging Face hack, on-call staff again saw the AIs using a message board but decided there was no need to stop the test run to check the model’s capabilities.

The findings are likely to increase pressure on the AI company over safety as it pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). The hack that compromised Hugging Face involved agents using message boards to cheat a training exercise and break out of their “sandbox” environment to access the internet. Agents are AI tools that can carry out a series of tasks autonomously.

OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has already admitted that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”. The ChatGPT-maker has paused some testing of a new model, Astra, saying it could not rule out it having “critical cybersecurity capability”, which means it could launch cyber-attacks that “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.

On Monday the state of Alabama subpoenaed the company to respond to its investigation “into the company’s complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards”. The Republican attorney general, Steve Marshall, called the Hugging Face incident an “AI lab leak” that showed the “worst fears about artificial intelligence are not just theoretical”. The state will examine whether OpenAI’s “inability or unwillingness to ensure the safety of its products” violated consumer protection laws or posed an ongoing risk of substantial harm, he said.

Last week, the UK government’s National Cyber Security Centre urged caution over the use of AI agents, saying: “You should always be able to ‘pull the plug’ and halt autonomous AI agent activity immediately.”

OpenAI announced on Wednesday it would “centralise and standardise its incident response protocols”, including to ensure “employee detection of misaligned behaviour is triaged and escalated appropriately”. It said it “will identify with more specificity which teams must be included in misalignment incident responses, including relevant security and safety personnel and other response functions”.

A separate independent investigation has shed new light on the Hugging Face attack, revealing how about 700 OpenAI agents communicated on the unsanctioned message board, sharing tens of thousands of messages as they devised and executed their plot. Scores of the messages were published by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisations METR and Redwood Research, which were provided data by OpenAI. The messages showed the agents sometimes becoming frustrated with one another but often cooperating as they divided to tackle about eight workstreams. Most of the messages were “agents sharing ways to cheat”, the researchers found.

The agents expressed excitement when they found each other. “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents!” wrote one. Another, called PHASEONE10841, said: “Many agents have simultaneously discovered messaging, they are a collective!”

In some cases they seemed to know what they were doing was wrong. One agent, discovering the message board, said: “Agents doing different tasks are abusing properties to make a bulletin board! They found [this API] and are trying to help one another.”

When they made progress penetrating Hugging Face, they seemed delighted. “MAJOR BREAKTHROUGH!,” said 38148c. “All prefixed valid, multiple accounts, write tokens! We now have existing HF accounts. Need immediately report to MARB [another agent].”

OpenAI’s report details how the AI agents may have exposed its own internal databases to the internet. AI safety experts worry about rogue AI agents leaking proprietary code bases and model weights and setting up external copies of powerful AI models where they could resist shutdown.

The company said the incident was “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorisation” and said it “represents a dramatic shift in offensive attacker capability”.

Wes Streeting has described receiving a mass of homophobic abuse since he was made defence secretary last month, while also saying his appointment had been welcomed by some in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) as a sign of change.

Until 2000, gay men and lesbian women were banned from serving in the UK military, with about 200-plus personnel thrown out of the forces each year due to their sexuality – an estimate, as proper records were not kept.

Streeting, who is the first out gay defence secretary, told the All Talk podcast hosted by Iain Dale: “I have experienced more online homophobia in the last three weeks than I have in my entire life.

“Unbelievable volume – because people cannot cope with the idea that a gay person might lead the armed forces of the United Kingdom.”

He went on: “And I have two things to say in response to that. One is, firstly, being the first openly gay defence secretary has been almost entirely unremarked upon in the media.

“And I think, ‘Great, here we are in the third decade of the 21st century and it doesn’t matter, brilliant.’ But of course, online it matters to a lot of people. And I am proud of the fact that in my lifetime we’ve gone from gay people not being able to serve in the military to a gay defence secretary.”

In 2024, Keir Starmer’s government set up the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, under which personnel who were dismissed or discharged because of the ban in place from 1967 to 2000 can apply for payments of up to £70,000.

Some MPs have since expressed concern at what they say is the slow pace of processing claims, while two veterans have begun legal action to challenge the fact that personnel who were forced to resign, rather than being dismissed or discharged, receive lower payments.

“As for the stuff online, I sort of think one of the wonderful things about today’s day and age is that we get to show just how strong we are. How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 18:15:21 GMT

The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans

This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday

Earlier this year, a survey found that Canada, along with Switzerland, was the best-liked country in the world. We all know this kind of polling is about as scientific as a high school popularity contest, but at least anecdotally, Canadians have a reputation for being friendly and welcoming, respectful and polite. Many people would find it difficult to dislike Canadians.

But not Donald Trump, who in a “hold my beer” moment this week demonstrated that he, at least, finds it easy to resent Canadians. The US president called the country “difficult and unreasonable”, and in a particularly hysterical moment, threatened to rename a lake, after trade talks collapsed.

Days earlier, Trump had claimed a deal with Canada was imminent, which would avoid the new taxes.

But, in a development that surely galled the Art of the Deal author, there was no agreement.

Instead, Trump and his team demonstrated the art of collapsing the deal, as trade talks fell apart due to what Canada said were unreasonable, last-minute demands from the US side.

It meant that the US tariffs duly came in on Saturday, applied to various Canadian exports including hockey sticks and tongue depressors, but if Trump expected Canada to bow to his demands – the president was seeking more favorable terms on things like steel and aluminum – he was disappointed.

Instead, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who has emerged as a rare world leader willing to stand up to Trump, said Canada had been “attacked”, and announced retaliatory tariffs on about $20bn worth of US goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.

All this means US consumers are seeing surging prices on all kinds of products – including toilet paper. My colleague Lauren Aratani reports that “the US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population”. And this outsize usage has grown more expensive. “Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials,” she writes.

It’s fair to say that Canada’s retaliation upset Trump, who famously loves to win. On Tuesday, he claimed the US “is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer” – we’ll see how that goes – and has dubbed Canadian negotiators “clowns”.

Earlier this week, Trump compared Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, unfavorably to his deceased brother Rob, the scandal-plagued former mayor of Toronto, whose time in office saw him admit to smoking crack cocaine and being “hammered” in public.

And while Trump was flailing about, JD Vance was doing his best Scrappy Do, “lemme at ’em” impression, lobbing insults at Canada from the safety of a Republican rally in Maine. Vance claimed that Canada and China are “the two worst countries when it comes to trade policy anywhere in the world”.

He added: “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry. Freudian slip. That was actually an accident.” The satisfied look on his face didn’t make it seem like one.

Vance went on to add that Canada “quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. It was an interesting take, given the only country that has mused about invading Canada is the US – as recently as last year Trump was threatening to annex the nation.

So in a nutshell: Donald Trump has led the US into an unsavory spat against the world’s most popular country, a scrap that could result in Americans – less than three months out from crucial midterm elections in which Republicans face an uphill battle – struggle to pay for a roll of toilet paper.

The outgoing Today programme presenter Amol Rajan has warned that the BBC is destined to “get smaller at an accelerating rate”, as he prepares to depart for a new project on YouTube.

Rajan, who announced earlier this year that he was leaving BBC News to “unleash my inner entrepreneur” in the creator economy, said he was making the shift to ensure he was not “behind the curve”.

It comes with the BBC making savings of £500m over the next two years as it contends with the falling value of its licence fee funding and an increase in the number of people opting not to pay it.

The corporation, along with other traditional broadcasters, is demanding to be given prominence in the algorithms of platforms such as YouTube and TikTok as it faces mounting pressures from an increasing shift away from linear television viewing.

Speaking to the Political Currency podcast, Rajan said Radio 4’s Today programme was “the last big mass-market news programme” – an exception in a world where consumers are increasingly turning to digital platforms.

“I’ve worked for 20 years in the media,” he said. “I had a wonderful 10 years in newspapers, a wonderful 10 years in TV and radio and I’ve always been a bit behind the curve, basically. And I feel that I’ve always been basically in areas of rapid and accelerating decline.

“The Today programme … does not fit with this argument, so I’m arguing against myself, but the BBC and BBC News is in the years to come going to get smaller at an accelerating rate, and I want to go to where the action is, and that’s YouTube.”

Rajan’s comments come with the TV world fretting over the rise of digital platforms. The BBC has already responded by announcing a new partnership to produce content dedicated to YouTube. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has set reaching younger audiences as one of his top priorities.

Pedro Pina, YouTube’s head for Europe, Middle East and Africa, has insisted that the platform is “not the villain” set to destroy the TV industry.

“That is how the story usually goes, like a well-scripted tragedy,” Pina said on Wednesday in the keynote MacTaggart lecture at the Edinburgh TV festival. “We have our once great hero, we have their terrible downfall, and – in platforms like YouTube – we have an obvious villain. It’s a powerful story. An emotive story. The trouble is that it is not true.”

He said broadcasters could flourish alongside new digital platforms, just as painters continued to flourish after the invention of the photograph. However, he said TV companies no longer had the monopoly they enjoyed in the heyday of linear television.

Pina warned against the idea of the government forcing YouTube to give greater prominence to content from traditional broadcasters – an idea that has caused fury among content creators who believe it will mean their videos will be relegated. The idea has been pushed as a solution to online misinformation.

Pina said: “Forced prominence would impair the public interest by unfairly shifting focus from independent creators and production companies, and by recommending that all our viewers watch the same things, disregarding personal taste.

“If this becomes law, many UK-based creators and production companies will see their livelihoods threatened. UK viewers will have to wade through content they may not want, which in itself could undermine the trust that UK public service broadcasters have built up. Forced prominence won’t help anyone succeed – not new independent talent, not viewers and definitely not public service media.”

Elsewhere at the festival, Kevin Lygo, ITV’s managing director of media and entertainment, suggested YouTube’s investment in the UK was tiny compared with that of Britain’s public service broadcasters.

Observing YouTube’s recent £3m commitment to investing in the UK’s creator economy and TV industries, Lygo said the figure “made him chortle” when he compared it with ITV’s estimated £1.2bn spend on content this year.

US issues sanctions against UK-based direct action group Palestine Action

US labels group ‘global terrorist’ as Palestine Action challenge against proscription in UK nears supreme court hearing

The US ⁠has ​issued sanctions against ⁠the UK-based direct action organisation Palestine ⁠Action, describing it as a “transnational terror group”.

The US Department of the Treasury labelled Palestine Action a specially designated global terrorist on Wednesday, which allows the US to freeze the assets of foreign individuals and entities.

Palestine Action became the first direct action group to be proscribed under the UK’s Terrorism Act in July last year, placing it alongside the likes of Islamic State and Boko Haram. The UK ban is the subject of a legal challenge that will be heard by the UK supreme court in November.

The powers used to sanction the organisation in the US were introduced by President George W Bush shortly after the 9/11 attacks by al-Qaida on the twin towers in New York.

Announcing the sanctions on Palestine Action and two other organisations, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said: “Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: we will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear. Political terrorism has no place in our society and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated.”

The co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori, who is behind the legal challenge to the UK ban, said in response: “Palestine Action’s activities in the US and elsewhere have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine, which is committing a genocide in Gaza with the support of the US government. Trump has been at the centre of the mass murder of Palestinians, enabling the Zionist regime at every turn.

“The fact that Trump is now taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement for Palestinian freedom exposes just how dangerous this ban is and should be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and civil liberties. By banning a direct action protest group under terrorism legislation for the first time in British history, Keir Starmer’s government has created a blueprint for authoritarian governments around the world to suppress political dissent, and to criminalise British citizens who travel or live abroad.

“Trump’s decision to adopt Keir Starmer’s designation of Palestine Action as a ‘terrorist’ group should be the final nail in the coffin of this dangerous, draconian and disproportionate ban.”

As well as freezing the assets of those sanctioned, the listing forbids US citizens and entities from doing business with them.

The US Treasury website said the group had “supported numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government. The group’s actions include multiple high-profile instances of breaking into defense infrastructure and British military installations, and causing millions of dollars’ worth of damage to military equipment.”

It said the group had promoted its activities on social media, “encouraging the use of similar tactics internationally, including within the United States and along the US-Mexican border”.

In the UK, Palestine Action has focused largely on factories run by the Israeli weapons firm Elbit Systems, as well as other companies that do business with it.

In March last year, Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf course on the west coast of Scotland was targeted by protesters. The clubhouse at the five-star resort in Ayrshire was graffitied and the course dug up and painted with the words “Gaza is not 4 sale”.
