The Guardian view on electoral reform: don’t wait for a crisis to fix a broken system

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 17:30:18 GMT

In an era of multiparty politics, first past the post risks generating perverse outcomes that delegitimise the democratic process

If the system that elects MPs to Westminster was obviously the most democratic one available, there would be no need to use alternative modes when electing the UK’s devolved assemblies or England’s regional mayors. The fact that first past the post (FPTP) was not preferred when establishing those institutions reflects an acceptance that there are better ways to turn popular opinion into fair political representation. So why should the Commons stick with an inferior system?

This question is raised by an amendment tabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament next week. The call to establish an independent national commission on electoral reform has been endorsed by 185 MPs.

Andy Burnham has backed electoral reform in the past and, as the Guardian reported this week, pressure is growing on the prime minister to translate that view into action: 98 Labour MPs have signed the amendment. For technical reasons related to the scope of the bill, the electoral reform question is unlikely to be put to a vote, but the scale of backbench support compels the prime minister to reaffirm his commitment to change.

Downing Street has made it clear that Mr Burnham does indeed back reform but, in deference to the manifesto he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer, accepts that there is no mandate to legislate this side of a general election. That is the constitutionally proper position, but it doesn’t preclude steps that will help win the argument when the time comes. Electoral reformers are haunted by defeat in the 2011 referendum on switching to the alternative vote model – a flawed rival to FPTP that was opposed by the Tories, then the senior party in coalition with the Liberal Democrats. The Labour party in opposition was divided.

Back then, the two largest English parties expected their duopolistic hold on Westminster to continue indefinitely. They had few incentives to change a system that suppresses small-party representation. What suited Labour and the Conservatives did not tally with voter preferences, as demonstrated by a steady trend of fragmenting allegiances.

Opinion polls show Labour, the Conservatives and Reform UK jostling for support at levels between one-fifth and one-third of national vote share. In devolved and local elections, the Greens, Liberal Democrats and Scottish and Welsh nationalists complicate the picture still further.

With multiple parties polling within a few points of each other, FPTP can propel a candidate to victory on a tiny margin and against the wishes of a clear majority of voters. This is a recipe for chaos and disenchantment – conditions that British politics has endured too much in recent years.

Delivering stable government is supposed to be a virtue of FPTP. Another is the link between MPs and their constituents, although elements of this can be retained with hybrid systems that also have a proportional element, such as multimember constituencies or combined list and constituency ballots.

There is no perfect voting system, but the potential pitfalls of alternatives are not a good enough reason to stick with a status quo that threatens such a perverse outcome as to delegitimise the democratic process. The clamour for reform would then be irresistible. Preparations to modernise the way parliament is elected, and win public support for change, should begin well before that crisis point is reached.

The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 17:25:18 GMT

There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock

Every minute, 23 girls around the world wed, according to the Girls Not Brides campaign, a coalition of more than 1,000 organisations across 100 countries. No child should be married. But girls are far more likely to be affected than boys, accounting for nine in 10 of those wed before 18, and their spouses are often much older men. The consequences, beyond the immediate threat of sexual violence, include the shortening of their education, increased risks of poverty and domestic abuse, and poor health, including high rates of maternal mortality. In spring, the Center for Global Development thinktank estimated that child marriage costs $175bn annually in lost productivity and increased health risks.

The good news is that the last decade has seen a drop in rates; last year alone, Grenada, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Kuwait and Portugal introduced bans. But there are disturbing signs of regression elsewhere. In May, the Taliban issued a new judicial code enabling child marriage below the previous minimum age of 16, and preventing wives from ending marriages they entered as children if their husbands object. Previous protections were inadequate and often poorly enforced; now even those have been swept away. Activists say forced and early marriages have soared since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, thanks to the ban on secondary education and the state of the economy.

Child marriage is almost double the global average in countries experiencing conflict or other crises, with more than one in three girls marrying before they turn 18, Girls Not Brides reports. The breakdown of economic and support systems, and the exacerbation of factors driving child marriage, such as patriarchal values, can leave families seeing marriage as the only way to protect their daughters – even though they frequently face violence from their husbands. In Gaza, the rate of child marriages dropped from more than 28% in 2009 to just under 18% in 2022. The war has reversed that progress, says the UN Population Fund, with case workers reporting steeply rising rates.

Yet child marriage happens in the developing world too. Under-18s could marry in all 50 states of the US until 2018; 17 states have now passed bans, but three – New Mexico, California and Mississippi – still have no age floor. England and Wales raised the minimum age to 18 in 2023; in Northern Ireland, those aged 16 and older can marry with parental consent, and in Scotland they can marry without it. In Australia, 16- and 17-year-olds may marry “in exceptional circumstances”.

There is still cause for optimism. Although laws are often evaded – sometimes through corruption, more frequently because marriages are not officially registered – they still send an important message. In Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024, the first trial has begun over the forcible marriage of a 17-year-old. Four men, including the girl’s father and alleged groom, face jail sentences of at least 15 years or fines. The new law allows even guests at the wedding of a child to be imprisoned.

Advocacy targeting girls as well as their communities is essential, helping some to resist marriage. Cuts to overseas aid now threaten such work. Child marriage will not end until girls also have educational and economic opportunities, reproductive healthcare and some measure of security. This must be a priority.

Whimsical shortlist announced for Edinburgh comedy award 2026

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 17:23:39 GMT

A shortlist rich in kookiness sees Lara Ricote tipped for the main prize, alongside returning nominees and a new generation of eccentric fringe acts

The shortlist has been announced for the annual Edinburgh comedy award, and it’s a list that majors in whimsy. With an act hymning his belief in healing crystals, another dreamily counting sheep and a third whose show is about “mystery and messages” – and that’s before we even get to the loopy DIY comedy of TV veteran Spencer Jones – this year’s “Oscars of comedy” nominees (for both the best show and best newcomer prize) suggest an art form exploding with creativity but also increasingly oriented towards woo-woo: in full flight, perhaps, from our troubled times.

The award favourite is Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote, co-star of Sam Campbell’s Channel 4 mockumentary Make That Movie and former fringe best newcomer. Ricote’s Inkling is a remarkable hour about picking up on the messages that come one’s way, and how that’s complicated by, in the 29-year-old’s case, being hard of hearing.

Returning to the annual shortlist, for an award once known as the Perrier, are Chris Cantrill (a three-time nominee whose double act sidekick Amy Gledhill won in 2024), shouty Mancunian Dan Tiernan (nominated twice before) with Quartz and All and goofball prop comic Jones (also nominated twice before). Jones is the veteran of this year’s list with his own BBC show, The Mind of Herbert Clunkerdunk, already under his belt.

On a shorter list than we’ve seen in recent years, they are joined by Cornwall’s Harriet Dyer, recently announced as a participant in the Halloween edition of Amazon Prime’s smash hit Last One Laughing UK, and whose show Easily Distra … celebrates her inability to stay on topic; and Li Jin Hao, the UK-based Singaporean whose show Falling from a Moon develops the brand of woozy philosophical comedy pioneered in his 2024 show Swimming in a Submarine.

The most egregious omissions from the lineup, which is selected by industry and public panellists, are Elf Lyons with The Woman on the Edge, an extraordinary breakup show that’s got everyone talking; Aussie stunt-comedy offering Man Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour; and the Radio 4 sketch trio Crybabies with their brilliantly executed horror pastiche The Scaring.

On the best newcomer shortlist – for an award previously won by Sarah Millican, Tim Minchin and Harry Hill – there’s more whimsy still. Too many kooks, you might say, at a festival where socially engaged or political comedy is vanishingly thin on the ground. Or you could celebrate the surfeit of invention among acts that include Limerick’s Marty Gleeson, a quartet of US clowns performing their Underground Monk Show, and Birmingham teacher turned oddball Tom Towelling, with a show that binds its audience together in wool.

Completing the newcomer nominees, at a time when the proficiency of first-time Edinburgh acts seems to be rocketing, there are Dom McGovern with Prize Hog, TV regular but fringe rookie Fatiha El-Ghorri with Cockney Stacking Doll, Freddie Meredith with the terrific Need a Light? and Omar Badawy with Guided Detour.

Chair of the judging panel Liz Lewin, director of comedy series at Netflix UK, said of the lists: “These are the people shaping the comedy landscape and we can’t wait for audiences beyond Edinburgh to enjoy them as much as we did”. The awards will be handed out at a ceremony this Saturday by 2016 winner Richard Gadd and last year’s best newcomer and now SNL:UK star Ayoade Bamgboye. The winners will receive £10,000 for best show (sponsored by Audible), and £5,000 for best newcomer. Recent winners of the main award include Rose Matafeo, Hannah Gadsby and last year’s champ Sam Nicoresti.

Rebecca Hendin on the legacy of Dolly Parton – cartoon

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 17:11:39 GMT

Read original article

Affairs? Drugs? You could ask Dolly Parton about anything and get a laugh. Just stay away from politics …

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 17:00:17 GMT

One autumn day in 2023 I bathed in the luminous glow of this utterly authentic star – and while she did have one weak spot, her life and music will speak for themselves

Celebrity tributes pour in for Dolly Parton

Dolly Parton’s 10 best deep cuts

Alexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless career

The great privilege of my kind of journalism is to get the chance to meet extraordinary people – some famous, many not – and very occasionally that person is beyond extraordinary. Dolly Parton, you may not be surprised to learn, was one of them. I’ve only come across it a handful of times. It has nothing to do with extreme fame – I’ve met plenty of A-listers who are dead behind the eyes. It’s not charm or extroversion either, nor beauty, and it’s not what we’d call “star quality” because it’s less showy than that. It’s almost indescribable, but “luminous” probably comes closest. I think it’s partly innate – God-given, Parton might have said – but it also comes from living with humility, gratitude and humour. Parton was luminous, and it wasn’t just the rhinestones.

The cliche that you should never meet your heroes because you’ll only be disappointed only stands if you think famous people have somehow transcended the deep character flaws that make the rest of us human. Everyone has off days, or off years. Still, I’d been slightly dreading interviewing Parton. The machinery that surrounds a superstar interview – the holding rooms, the allotted time slots, the officious publicists – is designed to be intimidating, and it was all present on that autumn day in 2023. And then it was just Parton and me in a London hotel room, borderline uncomfortably close on a sofa, but unusually, no publicist sitting in, taking notes.

She was funnier than I expected, and warmer. Parton’s artifice – the look, the folksiness, the ready quips – was clearly part of her armour. You can deflect any tricky question, or criticism, with a well timed boob joke. But somehow it didn’t feel fake. It was her creation, but it was still her. I had no illusions I’d get to the real Parton, whatever that was, in our hour together – she even went to bed with her makeup on, she said, because she didn’t want to go to bed “looking tacky” for her husband.

Certain things don’t make it into interviews because written down they look trite, or lose power, but re-reading my transcript, I think I underestimated how spiritual Parton was. “You need to believe in something bigger than yourself,” she said. “You need to believe in at least a higher power, the higher wisdom, whether you call it nature or whatever, to get you out of yourself.” She would often break into reciting her lyrics (“Whatever you are, be that / Whatever you do, do that / Everything else is just an act”) which, in person, felt like being preached to by a beatific being.

She could deal, with humour and grace, with the sort of questions other celebrities – or at least their PRs – would throw you out for. Had she or her husband had affairs? “If there [were], we don’t know about it.” Had she ever been tempted? “I didn’t say I’d never been tempted,” she said with a laugh. “I said I’m married, not dead. Nor blind.” We were meeting partly to discuss her book about fashion, and she’d written about partying at Studio 54: how many drugs had she taken? Nothing hard, she said. “I don’t really want anything to change me. I don’t want to mess with my brains.” It didn’t make my piece – even with follow-up questions, her deflection was too practised, her answers too opaque. It’s more an illustration that she was game.

The only thing that was off-limits was her politics. Much as I admired her, I thought this was Parton’s weak spot. Her apolitical stance seemed, to me, about protecting her career, her money. If you’re political, she said, “you’re gonna lose half your audience. I’ve got as many Democrats, as I do Republicans as fans, and I’m not going to insult any of them because I care about all of them.” It was the same reason she didn’t describe herself as a feminist, she said – she didn’t want to alienate men.

Sign up to Sleeve Notes

Get music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every week

after newsletter promotion

I needled her (she remained good-humoured) because it seemed a cop-out – this was 2023, and life had become frightening and intolerable for many people. Tennessee, her home state, had not long banned abortion in almost all cases. At what point does silence, given her platform, start looking like complicity? “I have my own opinion about everything,” she said, “but I don’t have to march in the streets for it, I don’t have to insult other people for it. I don’t think that makes me a hypocrite. I think it makes me a loving, caring human being.”

Three years on I’ve softened towards Parton’s refusal to add to the noise, to label herself, to take sides, to inevitably alienate and polarise and condemn. Deeds not words. Parton’s deeds – living as a feminist, if not calling herself one, and her philanthropy, and of course her music – speak for themselves. I had it for an hour in that hotel room, just the hack who happened to be chosen for that assignment, but we were all lucky to be touched by Parton’s light.

‘9 to 5? She was full-on round the clock!’ Dolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and more

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 16:46:45 GMT

Musicians and performers pay tribute to the country legend who managed to be a generational talent, a formidable entrepreneur, a dedicated philanthropist and a truly kind person

Shirley Collins, singer-songwriter

I don’t really follow pop music or country and western very much, but Dolly Parton was always something special – separate from it all, in a way. She seemed absolutely indomitable. Coming from a large family in a mountain home and being brought up in poverty, she broke through to have this incredible career and you couldn’t help feeling fond of her. How she did it I don’t know, but nothing seemed to faze her.

I was always impressed by her perception of things. Like in Jolene, the carelessness of someone taking someone’s husband “just because [she] can” is really clever. Dolly could see stuff and then write about it in ways that nobody else could.

A few years ago, someone sent me a book called The Pack Horse Library, about women in the Appalachians in the 1930s who rode pack horses or mules in this wilderness country and took library books to all the isolated cabins with huge families, who wouldn’t normally get near a library. In modern times, Dolly has done exactly the same thing, but on such a massive scale, posting books to children around the world. She wasn’t just a big-bosomed singer of great songs – and she wrote so, so many great songs – but a fabulous human being. I think we’re all really rather privileged to have been able to see her.

I wouldn’t talk like this about any other pop singer, but as a singer and a person she was in a class of her own. It’s a sad, sad day, but people will always think of her and smile.

kd lang, singer-songwriter

She was a plain-clothed prophet. She transcended all misconceptions of what a Christian is, what an American is, what an artist is or what an ally is. She came from a southern, Christian, country and western place and she never wavered in her support of the LGBTQ+ community or the Black community – all those that have suffered at the hands of those with a far-right mentality.

I believe in the divine timing of things and I think that, in her departure, there’s a gift, too, because I can’t think of anyone who had a more cohesive effect on people than Dolly Parton. Her exaggerated physical presence – her hair and her boobs and her hips and her clothes – was a caricature, one we sometimes laughed at. But the joke was on us, because she embraced who she was and never judged anyone else. She truly embodied that way of being – just live and let live.

Of all her songs, I really like Coat of Many Colors. I’m not a Christian, but there’s something so down-home about that. I truly believe that it is a story from Dolly’s life. She used the tools she was given and one of them was being from a large country family that was raised Christian. She took the very essence of the teachings and illuminated them to the highest degree. May she have a swift rebirth.

Joan Osborne, singer-songwriter

I had the honour of singing her song Do I Ever Cross Your Mind? for a Dolly compilation called Just Because I’m a Woman in the early 00s. During the recording session, she sent over a big, home-cooked meal, that she had made herself, to give to the musicians and me so we wouldn’t get hungry while we worked. When the album was done, she sent me a very gracious handwritten letter, saying that my version of her song had made her cry. I wish I could lay my hands on that letter right now. It’s buried somewhere in my archives. But I do remember it very well and someday I’ll unearth it and frame it for my studio.

I always admired the way that Dolly hid in plain sight. She was an immensely talented songwriter and beautiful singer, a serious artist and a brilliant businesswoman, but she wrapped herself in the disguise of a comic blond bombshell. Her presentation was probably a result, at least in part, of her desire to fulfil the fantasies of a little girl who grew up in poverty, but it was also a very smart career strategy.

Peggy Seeger, singer-songwriter

Dolly was a one-off – and I mean off the wall. Honest, brash, daring and way ahead of her time, yet very present in her own time. She wasn’t a 9 to 5 woman; she was full-on round the clock. I followed her career throughout and adored everything she did. She’s left us way too soon, yet left us so much.

Annie Lennox, singer-songwriter

On 5 November 2022, Eurythmics had the unforgettable experience of performing Jolene with the legendary Dolly Parton, joining alongside an exceptional mix of musical acolytes, representing a cross-section of musicians who were all being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. When we arrived for the dress rehearsal, there she was, standing centre stage, a surprisingly tiny figure in vertiginous high-heeled boots and full rocker regalia, dressed head to toe in a figure-hugging outfit of black skintight PVC, adorned with suspended pendants of silver chains. As tiny as she was, her presence was big enough to fill 10 football stadiums.

She was warm and personable, with a tremendously dry sense of humour. We all felt extremely favoured to be part of that song performance. It was a special moment with no pedestals in sight … except for the one we placed her upon that night.

Rest in power, Dolly Parton … the REAL deal.

Billy Bragg, singer-songwriter

We’ve lost someone who was an embodiment of a type of American exceptionalism that has been eclipsed by the Trump carnival of people who say: “Empathy is toxic.” She was the opposite of that. Her faith was based on the idea that, as she once said: “I just want everybody to be treated good.” That quote came from someone asking her about anti-trans legislation in her home state of Tennessee. She didn’t hedge it. She went on to say: “We are all God’s children and how we are is who we are.” She didn’t stop at trans people, or American people, or white people. She extended that to everybody.

When people are saying empathy is toxic, you need someone like Dolly Parton to come along like the Attack of the 50 Foot Woman and put them back in their box. Everyone talks about a divided America, but her superpower was to bring people together. She completely transcended her role and became a universal figure, a bit like the queen, and similarly the reaction to her passing has been exceptional.

Obviously, as a songwriter, she was incredible. Everyone knows about the great songs that have been all over the radio in the last 24 hours, but for me her artistry also lies in the more obscure songs such as Do I Ever Cross Your Mind? – the chord changes are to die for – or Down from Dover, a heartbreaking song where a young woman is pregnant and waiting for her boyfriend to come back. He doesn’t come and the baby dies. It’s a heart-rending song that doesn’t just put the position of unwed young women at the centre; it also plumbs into that great Appalachian tradition of tragedy songs, which she heard when she was growing up and will have seen first-hand.

She was tougher than any man. Her second album was called Just Because I’m a Woman. She was saying: don’t be messing with me, because I see through your pernicious attitudes towards me as a woman and I’m gonna turn that back on you. And she was incredibly powerful at doing that. She had kindness and empathy, but she wasn’t like a little flower. She had the strength to broadcast her empathy to the world. She was the epitome of that rhinestone, vaudeville, bouffant, over-the-top America that I’ve always been attracted to, but also the best of humanity. She really was the best of us.

Jonny Woo, drag performer

Everyone loved Dolly. How could you not? She was the archetype of joy and beauty and generosity – and the music was amazing. The first time she came into my psyche was watching her in 9 to 5 and she’s the best person I’ve seen at Glastonbury in 20 years of going. When she was talking, just in her normal voice, the crowd were absolutely silent. Her voice was immaculate. Her storytelling was just joyous. I think there were more people watching her than the Rolling Stones.

So, of course, my drag troupe and I all dressed up as her. That image is so joyous. It’s not derogatory to call her a camp icon. Like Céline Dion or Cher, she was very aware of the pleasure of her visual appeal. They’re celebratory and stylish, using their femininity and sexuality to lift your mood.

She said: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.” But on stage she was like a diamond: her music shone, her voice shone and her image shone. It’s just hard not to smile when you think of her.

Because she came from such an extraordinarily poor background, she could connect with the working-class experience around the world. She was interested in people: “Tell me where you come from. What’s your life about?” I don’t know how much country music embraces queer culture – possibly not much – but she was hugely supportive of us.

She was the kind of person who got on with it: did the job, got her money and helped people out, rather than making a big song and dance about it. She was strong without being aggressive and would rebut people without being unkind, which is a great skill. You just knew she had the back, not just of queer people, but of all people who face shit in their lives. She was looking out for you and singing for you. She’ll be hugely missed, but thinking of her immediately fills us with joy, rather than sadness.

KT Tunstall, singer-songwriter

Dolly was beyond the greatest. She was a world-leveller, in her immeasurable talent and in her ability to wrap anyone and everyone together in warmth and love. She’ll for ever be one of the best examples of how to spend a life on Earth.

Kelly O’Brien, ‘the world’s No 1 Dolly Parton tribute’

I don’t think I’ve had time to properly process Dolly’s passing. Every time I hear a bit of a song, it gets me started. I grew up in Australia. My parents would play her records and I’d go to sleep listening to Love Is Like a Butterfly and Jolene. As you get older, you think: “Wow, this woman’s clever. She’s no dumb blonde. She knows exactly what she’s doing.” Talking to interviewers, she would make fun of herself before anybody else could. From her entrepreneurism and humanitarianism to her philanthropy, she was a very clued-up woman.

I started mucking around being Dolly 30 years ago. Being Dolly takes a lot of practice. I really studied her voice a lot, because I wanted to represent her in the best way possible. That meant going on a very strict diet, learning the accent, learning all the songs, her mannerisms. The costumes had to be right and the wigs had to be perfect. I based my work on her perfection.

She means a lot to so many people in a world that’s gone a little bit mad. She’s this constant, kind, big-hearted, wholesome girl. She represented not only women, but anybody down on their luck, singing about unwedded women back in the early 70s and a world on fire. She reached a whole new younger generation of admirers when she performed at Glastonbury in 2014, because she was Miley Cyrus’s godmother and so glamorous.

She didn’t really approach politics, but then I think with her Rockstar album in 2023 she probably got a bit fed up and so became even more outspoken about LGBTQ+ rights and things like that. She used to have gay days at Dollywood and I think she used to get death threats, but she stood her ground. She’d go: “No, this is who these people are. They’re born this way. God accepts them and you have to do the same.” She brought some badass ideas to the deep south.

I met her in 2011, backstage at the O2. I was dressed as her – unexpectedly, we had matching gold outfits! – and we were the same height. It was terrifying, because I was going to meet my idol, but she said she loved what I did and loved all the drag queens and Dolly impersonators everywhere. It was just magical, which she was.

Paul Jepson, director of the musical 9 to 5

She was an extraordinary person and very talented. We wanted to honour her extraordinary spirit. Our show’s music supervisor, Mark Crossland, and choreographer got to know Dolly. She had a lot of involvement in the development of the musical. Obviously, it’s her songs [and was originally a Broadway production, based on the 1980 movie], but everyone commented on how incredibly generous she was. She recorded herself singing, and bits of speaking, and sent them down the line from the US. Afterwards, she would ask if we needed to make any changes or needed anything else. She was the consummate pro. People often make this stuff up, but she was genuinely lovely and everybody loved her.

One of the numbers in the show is Backwoods Barbie, which Karla Tracey – as Doralee – does exceptionally well. It’s actually a confession: she’s talking about where she comes from and she’s upset, because everyone has been horrible to her. Dolly got that: she was writing about something she knew very well with great eloquence and skill. A lot of people don’t know that the 9 to 5 song and movie was based on a real organisation, 9to5, that still exists and is still fighting discrimination and pushing for workers’ rights.

I’m very glad the show has been touring in places such as Worthing, Bridlington and Darlington, which aren’t known as primary dates for this level of attention. They’re places that haven’t always been shown a lot of love – a bit downtrodden, if you will – and we wanted to stand up for them. I’d like to think that Dolly would have approved. It seemed a very Dolly thing to do.

The Wiggles, children’s music group

We are heartbroken to hear of the passing of Dolly Parton. Dolly brought so much joy, kindness and music into this world and we feel incredibly lucky to have spent time with her and to have called her our friend.

Her extraordinary legacy goes far beyond the songs we all know and love. Dolly dedicated so much of her life to helping children dream big, including through her Imagination Library, which has put millions of books into the hands of children around the world.

Getting to make music with Dolly was something we will treasure for ever. But even more special was experiencing the warmth, generosity and joy that made her so deeply loved by generations of families. Thank you for the music, the laughter, the stories and everything you did for children everywhere. We will always be friends. We love you, Dolly. Rest peacefully.

The London stock market dodged a bullet with Shein

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 16:21:36 GMT

China’s fashion giant will list in Hong Kong with a shrunken price tag – and big questions over its business model

In a parallel world, we might now be preparing for the arrival on the London stock market of Shein, the giant Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer. Or it could have happened already.

The possibility of a London flotation was a running story during 2024 and into last year as politicians from both main parties engaged in behind-the-scenes wooing. Shein was seen as a shot of tech adrenalin for a listless local listings scene, and an opportunity to advertise the UK’s openness to international capital.

Instead, Shein will float next week in Hong Kong. To which one can only say: thank goodness for that.

In a listings context, Shein was a cast-off. The company had rejected New York amid tensions between Washington and Beijing and hostile questions from US lawmakers over labour practices in its supply chains in China. London was merely the next-best option for a company whose owners seemed suspiciously anxious to find a stock market home in the west.

London did its reputation no favours with its willingness to jump. The Financial Conduct Authority, in charge of listings, took the view that it was “not unusual” for UK-listed companies to carry legal risks around the world and that what mattered was disclosure to allow investors to form their own view. The Labour government sounded keen. Donald Tang, the banker hired as Shein’s chair, did a round of feelgood meetings.

This positivity was punctured, however, in January last year when Shein’s general counsel in Europe appeared at the Commons business select committee and stone-walled.

Did Shein source cotton from China, asked the committee chair, Liam Byrne. The company representative was not qualified to reveal such “detailed operational information”. Byrne had not even been asking at that point about allegations of use of cotton produced in the Xinjiang region, which has been linked to Uyghur forced labour.

The company, it should be added, had already said it had signed statements of compliance to modern slavery acts in the US, UK and elsewhere. But Byrne’s view was entirely fair: “The reluctance to answer basic questions has frankly bordered on contempt of the committee.”

The idea of listing in London soon went away – encouraged, it seemed, by pressure from Beijing. And so, Hong Kong it is.

Note, though, how the company’s price tag has shrunk from the £50bn that was talked about during the London leg of the global tour. The valuation will be $27bn (£20bn).

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

That figure also reflects the other issue that has dogged Shein: political and societal resistance to the practice of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods. The US has already closed such “de minimis” exceptions as part of President Trump’s tariffs wars; the EU says it will phase them out; the UK intends to get there by 2029. Shein used to argue that its business model did not depend on tax breaks, but the reduced valuation suggests that investors do not regard the issue as irrelevant.

In a world in which Shein had somehow managed to list in London last year, the valuation drop would have been felt here. The supposedly hot prize would look substantially less so. London dodged a bullet on this one. Those politicians who encouraged the flirtation might reflect that, while the stock market is obviously desperate for exciting newcomers, you’ve got to choose your targets carefully. Nobody is talking about a missed opportunity.

Deirdre McSharry obituary

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 16:10:39 GMT

Editor of Cosmopolitan in its 1970s heyday when it was famous for addressing women’s careers, health and their sex lives

Deirdre McSharry, who has died aged 94, edited Cosmopolitan in the magazine’s golden era. As fashion editor when the UK magazine launched in 1972, within a year she was elevated to the top spot. Under McSharry, “Cosmo” was witty and forthright, addressing women’s careers, style, health and, notoriously, their sex lives. Like its editor, it was guided by joie de vivre.

A 1973 documentary captured a conversation between McSharry and one of Cosmo’s occasional nude centrefolds. The model was irked – the centrefold showed him laughing. He preferred to smoulder.

As he explained to McSharry that women found a sultry look sexier, her smile broadened and her eyebrows rose. She knew better. The jollity of the centrefold was part of the point, she told the documentary crew: “For years, men have been picking up magazines with pictures of busty ladies, and we thought it was a good joke to simply reverse the role and make the man the sex object.”

For her team, she was a powerful inspiration and a formidable boss, not shy of criticism, but always interested in their lives and opinions. All were “Cosmo girls”, representing the magazine’s readership. They gathered weekly for editorial meetings and exercise classes. “What she couldn’t tolerate was lack of ambition,” recalls Pattie Barron, Cosmopolitan’s then health and beauty editor.

McSharry was ambitious for her staff in return: “It was typical Deirdre to push everyone to the max and then push them out of the Cosmo nest, never holding them back to keep working for her. She wanted to see us fly.”

Caroline Coon, a regular contributor in the 1970s, recalls the cultural impact of the magazine and its feminist editor: McSharry “promoted actual change that could be achieved, with a dollop of glamour and fun”.

She was born in West Ham, east London, to Mary (nee O’Brien) and Jack McSharry, an Irish doctor who worked with tuberculosis patients before succumbing to the disease himself. In 1939, newly widowed, Mary moved with her two children to Dublin. Deidre was sent to a convent school and her mother went to work, becoming editor of Woman’s Life magazine.

It came as a shock to realise that her schoolfellows pitied her for having a mother with a career. She “always made work seem very special and glamorous,” Deirdre recalled.

In the holidays, she and her brother Sean were taken to the theatre, to lunches at the Stephen’s Green Club, and to the magazine office, where Deirdre learned to type and to paste articles into the “dummy”. Her mother encouraged her to paint and steered her towards biographies of clever women. All this proved formative.

At Trinity College Dublin studying English, McSharry started to write and act. Her mother died just before she reached 21. She did not graduate but turned to the theatre, performing with the Dublin Players and in late-night revues at the Pike theatre. Throughout her life she retained the crisp diction and elegant poise of an actor.

Joining the Gate theatre under the founding directors Hilton Edwards and Micheál Mac Liammóir, she was part of the ensemble during a two-month tour in Egypt in 1956. The trip was a revelation, introducing McSharry to exquisite textiles and richly patterned designs that became an enduring obsession.

Following a brief marriage to Linton Stone in 1955, McSharry moved to New York. There she made a definitive shift from theatre into journalism, with a role on Women’s Wear Daily.

Later in the 1950s she moved to London as a fashion writer. A photograph shows her modelling an Aran jumper for a magazine shoot – the reverse carries a wry note that she was “saving the price of a model for George Newnes, publisher of Woman’s Own (circulation 4m)”. That figure was no exaggeration. In 1958, Time magazine cited “Britain’s proliferating women’s weeklies” as having a collective circulation of 10.4m. The newspapers paid attention: McSharry was lured on to the Daily Express as fashion editor.

She was a natural tastemaker, curious and enquiring, confident in her judgment. In 1966, she so liked the look of a model used for a daringly short haircut by Leonard’s of Mayfair that she called her in to the Express and commissioned a shoot. McSharry’s headline proclaimed the teenager, dubbed Twiggy, “the face of 1966”.

She married her second husband, Peter King, in 1967. The end of that marriage, in 1984, caused a period of ill health that precipitated her departure from Cosmo. After recuperating, in 1985 she became founding editor of Country Living, a magazine that reflected an era of growing affluence and social mobility in the UK.

McSharry identified a middle-class readership for whom renovating rural property was aspirational. She promoted eclectic, inventive interior schemes that were understood as expressions of their owners’ personalities. Designers, makers and artists she admired were promoted both on the page and off. After encountering Candace Bahouth at the Crafts Centre in Covent Garden, the artist made frequent appearances in Country Living and became a close friend. Kevin McCloud, then a lighting designer, recalls her as “a sparkling and tireless champion of other people”, and admits that his “career in no small part started thanks to her”.

McSharry was twice awarded editor of the year by the Professional Publishers Association – in 1981 for Cosmopolitan, and in 1987 for Country Living. In the mid 80s she met Ian Smyth, with whom she lived in a sequence of beautiful homes in the UK and US, before settling in Bath, where she became a cornerstone of the city’s cultural scene. The couple married in 1999 and remained devoted until Smyth’s death in 2022.

McSharry is survived by her sister Mary and her brothers Sean, Harry, Frank and James, and by her stepchildren Matthew, Lucy, Malachi and Patrick.

Deirdre Mary McSharry, magazine editor, born 4 April 1932; died 14 August 2026

ADHD is no myth – but we should interrogate it all the same

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 16:06:28 GMT

Readers respond to Gina Rippon’s criticism of a controversial TV documentary about attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

Three months ago, at 42, I was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Unlike many adults prior to receiving a diagnosis, I had not spent years wondering whether I had ADHD. In fact, I was oblivious until quite recently, when I strongly identified with several things a colleague said about their own experience of ADHD. The more I learned, the more I found myself thinking: “Wow, that’s me.”

My forgetfulness, distractibility, messiness, chronic need for organisation and memory strategies, constant lateness, tendency to lose things daily, persistent perfectionism and habit of going, tyres screeching, right up to the last minute of every deadline suddenly made sense. Things I had spent my life viewing as daily frustrations or personal failings had an explanation. I had ADHD, and had always had it. There was a reason for the constant chatter and noise in my brain, with any gaps filled with, or interrupted by, a song. Honestly, literally anything can trigger a song.

The diagnosis brought an unexpected, enormous sense of relief. I could finally look at aspects of myself that I had previously been frustrated by and understand them differently – with a new kindness toward myself. And then I heard about a documentary claiming that ADHD isn’t even real, as discussed in Gina Rippon’s article (There is nothing scientific about The Great ADHD Myth? ‘documentary’, 20 August). My first reaction was confusion. Then embarrassment. Then actual shame. Had I just been a fool? Was the explanation that had brought me so much relief actually all just fiction?

Of course, it is healthy and worthwhile to question shaky science where the evidence is lacking. But to question the existence of a condition supported by decades of clinical research and scientific evidence is astonishing – and potentially so damaging to so many lives. For people like me, this isn’t an abstract argument about a trend or fashion. An ADHD diagnosis can fundamentally change how you understand your entire life.

I hope the documentary will continue to be thoroughly challenged. People who have found a framework for understanding and accepting themselves deserve better than to have that understanding so casually and thoughtlessly undermined by a documentary lacking even basic scientific rigour. Daisy JonesBristol

In her critique of the recent Channel 4 documentary on ADHD, Prof Gina Rippon apparently thinks that, when addressing the issue of how much validity the diagnosis has, all we need do is gather more scientific evidence about it. But huge amounts of evidence have already been accumulated. What she fails to consider is the question of how existing evidence should be interpreted, because she seems to assume that the status of ADHD as a genuine neurological disorder is indubitable. However, any body of data can be open to different interpretations. Moreover, she does not consider the fact that much research on ADHD has been conducted with the assumption that it is a distinct disorder and, unsurprisingly, has achieved results that support this. This assumption needs to be questioned, and there is nothing unscientific about doing so.

Prof Rippon also criticises the case study of Mason, used in the documentary, for not being a scientific experiment. But this implies a very narrow positivist view of what scientific inquiry involves. Single-case methodology, such as was used here, is scientific and has a long history of use in psychology, including neuropsychology. The salient question is the extent to which the results may be generalisable to a larger population. If sufficient such case studies are conducted with consistent results, stronger conclusions can be drawn. Dr Richard HassallHonorary research fellow, department of philosophy, University of Nottingham

An independent prevalence review which has taken into account all the research on childhood and adult ADHD will shortly be published, answering many of the issues brought up in this extremely biased programme. I would now urge Channel 4 to commission a much more accurate programme based on this review. It could be called ADHD: The Truth. Dr Val HarpinConsultant neurodevelopmental paediatrician

I was diagnosed with severe ADHD long before the current rise in adult diagnoses. I struggled profoundly to process and retain information at school and was moved back a year. At nine, I had to leave my prep school because of my learning difficulties. I was eventually accepted by Millfield school, where I was taught in very small classes.

My parents did not choose medication lightly. I was monitored by paediatricians for years and was also part of Prof Sir Michael Rutter’s English and Romanian Adoptees study following my adoption from Romania.

I am now 37 and run a successful dog-grooming business. In many ways, I found a life that suits the way my brain works: practical, creative, fast-moving and hands-on. But ADHD has not disappeared. Without medication, paperwork piles up, conversations become harder to follow and my organisation noticeably deteriorates.

I completely support careful diagnosis and sensible prescribing, and I understand concerns about overdiagnosis. But there is a difference between occasionally feeling distracted and having difficulties severe enough to shape your entire childhood.

Medication did not suddenly make education easy. Even with it, following tasks, instructions and courses could still be difficult. I wanted to learn, but processing and retaining information remained a struggle and sometimes stopped me taking on new courses because I knew how overwhelming they could become.

But medication gave me the chance to find myself, discover what I was good at and build confidence.

It did not make me someone else. It gave me a better chance to become myself. Rosieanna EdelmanBath

As a 45-year-old recently diagnosed with ADHD, I find the central question of Max Pemberton’s Channel 4 documentary The Great ADHD Myth? – namely, whether ADHD is a genuine neurodevelopmental disorder, or simply a set of tendencies – somewhat extraneous.

It is not only schools that fail to accommodate brains or behaviours that are deemed untypical. Our entire economy is predicated upon the idea that competition rewards hard work – and while that is fine for adults who are able to focus consistently on the demands of work and life, it is ill-suited to those who are not. Thus, adults with an ADHD diagnosis are often forced to choose between protecting our creative, sometimes chaotic true selves – our “fun-ness”, as Mason, the boy in the programme, put it – and medication that can make us feel more stable and productive, but also flat and uninspired.

Yes, it feels dystopian to potentially overdiagnose and overmedicate kids. But it is a different type of cruelty to throw those same kids out into a world that is not designed for them, without the language to understand why they struggle or how best to cope. Simon LeeTunbridge Wells, Kent

Birds have an eerie association with death

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 16:06:16 GMT

Responding to an article in which birds comforted Helen Harris during bereavement, Angela Smith describes her own experience

Helen Harris’s experience (A moment that changed me: my husband died – and birds began behaving strangely towards me, 19 August) chimes with that of a friend of mine who had many close encounters with robins after the death of her father. She too had birds flying into her house as never before but, unlike Helen, she believed that this was the person’s spirit making contact.

My own association between birds and death is rather different. The day my mother-in-law died, a wren had flown into the window of the classroom where I taught, and I found it dead on the ground outside. When we took her ashes to be scattered in the sea, a pheasant hit the car windscreen and died.

Some years later, at school, a blackbird flew into a glass door and died. “I hope this doesn’t mean someone is about to die,” I said to another teacher, explaining why I thought it might. That evening, I discovered that a good friend had died at about the same time.

I can offer no explanation, but for me there does seem to be an association between birds and death. Visiting robins are more uplifting than birds sacrificing their own lives, though. Angela SmithNorwich

Trump’s deep-sea mining plan flouts international law

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 16:06:05 GMT

Britain and other signatories to the UN convention on the law of the sea should protest against US proposal to lease seabed for mining, says Guy Standing

Your article on Donald Trump’s plan to lease millions of hectares of seabed in the Pacific for deep-sea mining correctly points to the ecological disaster that this could unleash (US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific, 24 August).

However, it does not mention that this plan contravenes international law in the form of Unclos, the UN convention on the law of the sea, which has been ratified by 171 countries and the European Union. The US has not ratified it, but since 1982 has agreed to abide by its rules and procedures.

Under Unclos, no deep-sea mining may be undertaken until an international code on environmental assessments has been agreed and, crucially, an international agreement has been reached on sharing the economic benefits among all countries. These have not been agreed by the International Seabed Authority, the body responsible for drawing them up.

The UK government, among 171 others, should protest vehemently at this reckless and lawless plan. Guy StandingAuthor, The Blue Commons: Rescuing the Economy of the Sea

Farewell, Dr Frank-N-Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go on

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 16:02:23 GMT

The versatile stage performer will always be remembered for his defining film role in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, which turned him into an icon of 70s underground cinema and proto-punk Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80 Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke and 50 years of stardom Clowns, corsets and kings – a life in pictures

Over the past decade, the issues of trans identity and gender fluidity couldn’t have been more contemporary, and Tim Curry was an integral part of what might be called their pre-history in pop culture. He was an icon – though maybe now a dimly remembered icon – of the 70s underground cinema and proto-punk.

Curry was a good-looking actor with a tremendous speaking and singing voice, and a versatile performer – he got Tony nominations for his varied stage work on Broadway as Salieri in Amadeus, Alan Swann in My Favorite Year (the part Peter O’Toole played on screen) and as King Arthur in Monty Python’s Spamalot. But it was his strange destiny to be remembered for one role: at once indelibly prominent and weirdly peripheral. He was the sensational Dr Frank-N-Furter in the thoroughly outrageous Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), the screen version of the 1973 stage show.

This was the drop-dead gorgeous “sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania” in mascara and fish-nets, a vampiric sex outlaw who challenges the dull complacency of the timid American teen couple, Janet and Brad, played by Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick. These hapless straights had got lost and found themselves in his exotic domain. Curry himself said that the movie stymied his film career for many years, because of typecasting in a role that could not really ever be repeated, and in fact a great deal of his income from screen work from then on derived from voiceovers. But he also hinted that it was a kind of pension, perhaps because of royalties from the million-selling soundtrack LP.

Curry defined the role, defined the movie, and helped define other things besides. Without Curry and Rocky Horror, there might be no Vivienne Westwood Sex boutique and no punk. He was a part of the sexual peacock movement that was upending the dullness and drear of the 70s. Curry swam briefly alongside Bolan and Bowie on a tide of glam.

There was something else. Curry described the awfulness of sitting with 20th Century Fox executives at early private showings of Rocky Horror and hearing the deathly silence that reigned in the screening room afterwards. But it was a smart young Fox publicity director, Tim Deegan, who realised what a draw Tim Curry and Rocky Horror could be in the burgeoning “midnight” circuit in New York. He booked the movie in, and its growing word-of-mouth success and audience participation rituals virtually created the underground cult film scene. The stylishly sexual Tim Curry drew in the crowds and created a market for movies such as Alejandro Jodorowsky’s El Topo, George Romero’s Night of the Living Dead, John Waters’s Pink Flamingos, Perry Henzell’s The Harder They Come, and David Lynch’s Eraserhead.

Tim Curry and Rocky Horror were wacky and campy: they grew out of the hokey B-movie tradition of sci-fi and horror. (One of Dr Furter’s lines is “We could take in an old Steve Reeves movie” – a tongue-in-cheek reference to the beefcake bodybuilder who starred in many daft sword-and-sandal movies after the war; he was the Schwarzenegger of his day, with a lively gay following.)

Furter was wildly popular, but it always threatened to box Curry into a niche image. Many actors find themselves through sheer random fate chained to some lucrative TV or soap opera role. But there is usually some chance of developing in other directions. Tim Curry’s screen career certainly stayed healthy enough, and he even enjoyed a kind of miniature version of his earlier cult celebrity in the wacky novelty murder-mystery flick Clue in 1985, based on the board game Cluedo, released with three alternative endings. Curry played the fruity butler Wadsworth, manically rushing about explaining everything.

But of course there could be no way of topping the extraordinary, brief impact of Dr Frank-N-Furter and Rocky Horror – not on screen anyway, although his stage musical work was admired for its variety. Curry’s Furter gave the world a blast of subversive fun.

Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 15:47:14 GMT

A prolific performer across stage, screen and TV, the actor starred in Legend, Clue and It, but will always be associated with the flamboyantly camp rock’n’roll musical in which he made his breakthrough

Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardom

Farewell, Dr Frank N Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go on

Clowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in pictures

Tim Curry, the versatile performer of screen and stage, who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died aged 80. Reports say Curry died at his home in Los Angeles.

The actor’s manager confirmed to Variety that he died peacefully. No cause of death is known as yet.

Ironically, Curry’s best-known roles all required a considerable physical transformation, to the extent that he was unrecognisable in all of them. Frank-N-Furter, Rocky Horror’s deranged scientist, saw him daubed in garish makeup and wearing stockings and suspenders, for the stage show (which debuted in 1973) and the film adaptation (released in 1975). In the Ridley Scott-directed fantasy Legend (1985), he was equipped with giant horns and scarlet skin as the Lord of Darkness. And in 1990, Curry was transformed with full-face clown pancake to play Pennywise in the TV miniseries It, based on the Stephen King novel.

Alongside these show-stopping incarnations, Curry enjoyed a successful parallel career in film, TV and theatre. Born in 1946, he earned a degree in drama and English from the University of Birmingham in 1968 and embarked on a stage career. His first significant role was in the original cast for the first West End production of the controversial musical Hair, in 1968 – where he met Richard O’Brien, who would go on to cast him in his own musical, The Rocky Horror Show. Curry went on to play Tristan Tzara in Tom Stoppard’s Travesties (taking over the role from John Hurt and Robert Powell), and Mozart in the Broadway transfer of Amadeus in 1980. Later highlights included King Arthur in the Broadway run of the Monty Python musical Spamalot.

Curry worked regularly in film, in roles including that of Robert Graves in Jerzy Skolimowski’s sinister The Shout, and later as Jeremy in the Ian McEwan-scripted political drama The Ploughman’s Lunch. Later, Curry found himself working largely in comedies – including Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, Muppet Treasure Island, Scary Movie 2, and McHale’s Navy – before providing voiceovers for numerous animated films, such as Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties, A Turtle’s Tale: Sammy’s Adventures and Ribbit.

Curry was also a regular presence on TV for more than four decades, playing William Shakespeare in John Mortimer’s six-part biography of the playwright in 1978, Bill Sikes in the 1982 US TV adaptation of Oliver Twist, and the wizard Trymon in the adaptation of Terry Pratchett’s The Colour of Magic in 2008. He voiced a stream of animated series (Duckman, Sonic the Hedgehog, The Mask and Star Wars: The Clone Wars) and was cast in many guest roles in established series, including Psych, Poirot and Criminal Minds.

“I’ve had the opportunities,” he said to the Guardian in 2025, “and I’m still showing up. You know? I think that’s what you have to do. You have to keep showing up.”

In 2012, Curry had a stroke while receiving a massage and received brain surgery. He was left with mobility issues and his short-term memory was also affected. “It was an odd thing, because my father had a stroke and died very soon afterwards,” he said. “I knew I had to force myself to relax and just take the opportunity to float a little.”

In 2025, he released his memoir Vagabond.

“I’m very aware that I’m lucky,” Curry said last year. “I’m astonished actually at how ambitious I’ve been. I didn’t think of myself as ambitious at all.”

Luke Evans, who played the role of Dr Frank-N-Furter in the recent Broadway production of The Rocky Horror Show, paid tribute on Instagram. The actor called him “a force, a bright fierce flame” and “an inspiration”. He added: “There will only be one Tim Curry.”

Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Susan Sarandon called him a “funny sexy original” in an online post. “Even wheelchair bound he continued to be so sweet and generous with his fans,” she wrote. “Thank you Tim for meaning so much to so many people.”

Carol Burnett, who starred with Curry in Annie, also paid tribute online. “Nobody could play lovable villains better than he could,” she wrote. “He was a dear friend. I was blessed to know him.”

Curry’s Clue co-star Michael McKean shared on X: “My last conversation with Tim Curry was about life and love and laughter. The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend.”

My mum has died – and there is one kind of response I can’t stand

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 15:40:07 GMT

The platitudes, euphemisms and cliches are excruciating. But the people who say nothing at all are the worst

Luckily, I already knew having a comic thought at a tragic moment is a natural stress response, or I might have worried. My mum has died, making me an orphan – and what first popped into my head was how annoyed Larry David would be.

In Curb Your Enthusiasm, when Marty Funkhouser’s mother’s wheelchair was run over by a car, he proclaimed himself an orphan. David informed him he was too old to be an orphan. Funkhouser insisted that if your parents are dead, you’re an orphan.

“You could be 70 and be an orphan?” David challenged.

“You could be 100 and be an orphan!’ Funkhouser maintained.

“You can’t be 100 and be an orphan.”

“Yeah, you can.”

“OK, Little Orphan Funkhouser,” concluded David.

Images of Annie-like red curls aside, the people who brought you into the world both having left it is pretty profound. I’m lucky to have a lot of support, but it’s a hard knock in life. A singularly specific brand of aloneness; the natural order that feels anything but. It’s so weird. There’s no one to tell me off any more, either. I wonder what I may get up to. What if I fall in with a bad crowd?

My mum “had a good innings though”, as I have been reminded roughly thrice daily. It’s been 14 years since my dad died, and there’s so much I’d forgotten about the grief game – namely the platitudes, the strange language, and how terrible so many of us are at dealing with it. The best reaction so far was a bloke who replied to my breaking of the news for sadmin purposes with: “OK, that’s fine.” At least he gave me a good story.

The main disclaimer here is that I do believe everyone is trying their best. It’s a serious minority who are deliberately attempting to offend or upset you “at this difficult time”. Most human beings are just hopeless at talking about death.

I also know that a lot of this is subjective. For example, it’s safer to err on the side of caution and use fluffy euphemisms such as “passed away” and “resting”. However, as a dyed-in-the-wool fan of simply saying “died”, that fluff grates. “Please accept my condolences” is ridiculous, because it sounds as if there’s a chance you might reply in the negative, outraged at the very idea. My least favourite is “I don’t know what to say” – and then a blank, expectant look, as though they are genuinely hoping you’ll provide a shortlist of suggestions. I’m also not that into “you have to be strong”. Because, why do I have to? The best way out is always through, surely.

But the absolute worst thing to say to the bereaved is nothing at all. Richard E Grant has spoken before about some longstanding friends who crossed the road to avoid him after his wife’s death. This week, he said that he’d never forgive them.

“I’m very unequivocal, black and white, all or nothing,” he said. “I’ve tried to go for the grey areas but it’s not succeeded for very long. There are people that have been edited out of my life and I will never see them again. If I had done that to them, I wouldn’t be able to look them in the face ... No, portcullis down, goodbye.”

What Grant endured was extreme, but most people who have “lost” (which sounds like absent-mindedly mislaying something) somebody have experienced the deafening sound of silence. You’re conversing with someone who doesn’t acknowledge the enormous way your universe has shifted, and it’s as if you’ve grown a second head that they pretend not to notice. Again, they’re almost definitely not doing it intentionally – they aren’t mentioning it because you seem OK right at this second (AKA you aren’t crying), and they don’t want that to change, or to remind you what’s happened, just in case you have completely forgotten. They mean well, and focusing on that fact is how you manage not to snap at them. (Grief can make you really tetchy, another aspect of it that had slipped my mind.)

So now I’m back in the sad saddle, a PSA that platitudes, euphemisms and cliches are excruciating. However, nothing is as awful as having to interact with somebody for whom all words on the subject have dearly departed. Even arguing about the age limit for claiming orphan status is better than that.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

With Nige still sulking, it was left to Honest Bob to unveil Reform UK’s latest ‘policies’

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 15:26:34 GMT

The sense of futility hanging over the room was almost overwhelming as Robert Jenrick took the stage

It’s turning out to be one of the longer sulks in Nigel Farage’s already sulk-filled career. Few politicians are better at having a strop and holding a grudge than Nige. At least on this side of the Atlantic. Donald Trump could give Farage a run for his money, but skin doesn’t come much thinner than Nige’s. He’s the soul of the Reform party as long as he’s the centre of attention and the yes-men and women – that’s everyone – around him are saying yes. But the moment reality challenges his narcissism, the mirror cracks.

There was a time when you couldn’t keep Nige away from a TV camera or a gathering of reporters. It’s what he lived for. But ever since the Guardian revealed his £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, Farage has gone all shy. Unable to bear the humiliation of being seen for the man he really is. The posh. The entitled. The venal. The grifter. Everything he has spent the last 25 years trying to persuade people he isn’t.

Even with the Reform party conference just over a week away and the pressure on him to be at his sparkling best, Nige is still playing hard to get. His one concession has been to give the softest of soft interviews to Jeremy Kyle, Reform’s pet stooge from TalkTV. When GB News is too challenging for Nige, then you know he is in a very delicate state. Nor is there any sign of his self-imposed exile having improved his frame of mind. His latest fantasy is that immigrants are on the verge of forming their own standing army and going to war with the UK. Not even Kyle could quite keep a straight face. Fever dreams all round.

So for the latest instalment of the Reform summer press conference-athon, we were back to Robert Jenrick. Back, because the front-of-house formalities have been almost exclusively left to him and Dicky Tice, and it was Honest Bob’s misfortune to have drawn the short straw on Wednesday morning. The sense of futility hanging over the room was almost overwhelming. Even had it been Nige on stage, the event would have been an uphill struggle. With Honest Bob at the helm it was dead in the water before he had said a word. Reform are tanking in the polls and, in any case, to see Honest Bob is to dislike him. A little goes way too far. The stench of opportunism is overpowering.

The purpose of the presser was supposedly to highlight Reform’s latest – unfunded, natch – promises to small business. Though as no one was really listening and were instead wondering what sins they had committed in a previous life to have to endure 45 minutes of a burbling, fantasy-driven Honest Bob, this was really a public demonstration of the sort of waste of time Reform was trying to save businesses from. Though its possible that someone in Reform HQ has recently developed a meta-brand of existential humour and is now actively toying with the media to see how long it is before anyone realises the party has nothing to say and no longer bothers to show up.

Honest Bob raced through the sell. A relaxation of the rules on data protection. Who cares if Big Tech get their mitts on your personal information? They will mine your data one way or the other, so we might as well make it as easy as possible for them. The VAT level for business would be raised to £150K and anyone kept on hold by HMRC for 30 minutes would be entitled to a £30 tax credit. Cue the whole country ringing HMRC at the same time just to save a bit of money. You don’t even have to listen to the music when you’re put on hold because no one is ever going to answer. Do this several times a day and you might never have to pay tax again.

This is personal for me, said Honest Bob. Look into my eyes. Trying to sound sincere. Though it’s hard to trust a man with a track record of betrayal and dishonesty. Nige, Dicky, Zia and Bob. All working-class boys from the wrong side of the tracks. It’s as if he had never read this speech before, passing it off as his own. The whole point of Reform is that everyone at the top of the party is posh and has absolutely no idea of what it’s like to have no money. Nor are they even on each other’s side, let alone that of small business. Zia can’t stand Honest Bob and Nige seems to hate everyone at the moment.

Then the final giveaway. Grandparents and parents would be able to invest £250k in a child’s business tax free. Because everyone has a quarter or a mill to spare. It was just delusional. Honest Bob doesn’t understand himself, let alone the average Brit. And don’t worry about where all the money to pay for all these giveaways would come from. Just offset them from the imaginary savings they had made from last week’s nonsensical pressers. Dicky Tice extolling the virtues of marital fidelity was quite the moment.

There was just time for a few questions. More out of habit than genuine inquiry. All of which merely exposed Honest Bob’s limitations. Like trying to pretend that the energy price increase had nothing to do with the war with Iran that Nige had insisted the UK would be better off joining. Then there were the polls which really, really didn’t show that the Reform surge had long since peaked. But there were moments of light relief, such as Jenrick going for Kemi Badenoch over her invented conversations with Giorgia Meloni. It takes one delusionist to spot another.

It took the reporter from the Press Association to mention the elephant in the room. The crushing sense of ennui. Please could Reform get around to talking about defence, foreign affairs and health, because they had long since exhausted all the topics for which they had spokespeople. Honest Bob hesitated. Reform not having any MPs it could trust on defence, foreign affairs and health should be taken as a sign of strength not weakness. No way was the party a reclusive one-man band. There was Dicky and Honest Bob after all. Not forgetting Honest Bob and Dicky.

‘Pack of lies’: Robert Jenrick launches personal attack on Kemi Badenoch

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 15:00:17 GMT

Reform MP seeks to heap pressure on Tory leader amid confusion around details of meeting with Giorgia Meloni

Robert Jenrick has accused Kemi Badenoch of telling “a pack of lies” about her meeting with the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, as he launched a deeply personal attack on his former boss.

The Reform UK MP sought to heap pressure on the Conservative leader amid confusion about whether Meloni urged Badenoch at a meeting in Rome to “be her own woman” and resist doing a deal with his party.

A Conservative spokesperson denied the party had suggested the Italian leader made such comments, after the Times initially reported she had. This was later removed from the newspaper’s report.

Jenrick described the leader of his former party as a fantasist. “It was obviously very, very embarrassing for Kemi Badenoch. My advice, if you go and visit a foreign leader, is don’t make up a pack of lies about what they say,” said Jenrick, who defected to Reform this year after losing out to Badenoch in a leadership contest.

The Tory leader met the Italian prime minister for an hour in a cafe in Rome on Monday morning and in a post on X afterwards she praised the handling of the Italian economy by Meloni, whose own Brothers of Italy party is under pressure from a new rival.

A spokesperson for Badenoch denied the Conservatives had made any false claims about the Meloni meeting, saying Reform was “just making things up” and “peddling conspiracy theories to distract [people]”. They went on to refer to the £5m gift the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, received from the Thailand-based businessman Christopher Harborne.

Jenrick said: “As regards Kemi, look, we could tell she was making it up. She lives in a fantasy of her own making. She made up that she got a degree offer from an American university for her CV, she claims she is going to be the next prime minister. There is a lot of fantasies going on at the moment in Kemi’s life.”

The university comment was a reference to a previous claim that Badenoch received an offer from Stanford University at the age of 16, which became the subject of controversy after former admissions staff said she had described an impossible scenario.

Jenrick and Badenoch featured in fresh claims this week that she had plotted with fellow Conservative cabinet ministers to remove Rishi Sunak as prime minister months before the general election.

A new book by Anthony Seldon alleges that after Jenrick resigned as immigration minister in 2023 over the details of Sunak’s plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, Badenoch discussed telling Sunak she would resign from the cabinet if he did not amend the policy, with some people recounting she “had promised she would ‘take him out’”.

Jenrick was speaking at an event in London where he announced a raft of polices including plans to scrap Britain’s data protection laws and widen a tax-relief scheme for investors in small businesses in the UK in an attempt to allow relatives to claim advantages more easily.

People on calls to HMRC who are left on hold for more than half an hour would get a £30 credit off their tax bill under Reform, Jenrick pledged, and he also announced plans to scrap the mandate for all new car and van sales to be zero-emission by 2035. “Let white van men choose the vehicle that they want to drive for their businesses,” he said.

Labour criticised Reform’s plans to replace GDPR with a “light-touch” privacy law modelled on New Zealand’s. “Robert Jenrick can’t say which important data safeguards he would scrap and whether it would put people’s personal details at risk. He’s making it up as he goes along,” a Labour spokesperson said.

Andy Burnham should rip up our undemocratic first past the post system – even if some in Labour disagree

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 15:00:16 GMT

Rearguard reactionaries may try to block the idea of a national commission into proportional representation, but we should want more not less democracy

A poll in the Mail on Sunday at the end of June was remarkable. It had not just Reform as low as 21%, but also Labour and the Tories. It was remarkable because it starkly demonstrated the fragmented landscape of the UK’s electoral terrain, as well as the electoral weakness of its main players.

Polls since have varied, not least with the Burnham bounce, but this week’s YouGov voting intention figures put Reform, Labour and the Tories on 23%, 22% and 20% respectively (although it almost no longer matters which exact figure applies to which party). Add in the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on 13% apiece, the SNP dominating Scotland and Plaid Cymru Wales, then Restore UK and independent candidates and you have an unprecedented variety of options laid out before the British electorate.

And all this despite the first past the post (FPTP) electoral system, which has for so long upheld two-party politics. It does so by punishing any party outside the duopoly by refusing to match votes to seats. If this unprecedented level of fragmentation exists in the face of a voting system that coerces people to back only their least bad option, then how diverse would this landscape be if people could vote with their heart and know that their vote really counted?

This now complete mismatch between what voters want and what they get is the root cause of the governing crisis destabilising British politics. Labour won two-thirds of the seats in the Commons in 2024 on just a third of the vote, and its leadership assumed that this result conferred it legitimacy in the eyes of the public. But governments increasingly find that a Commons majority upheld by an unrepresentative voting system is more vulnerable to voter backlash. In this context, support quickly melts away, as Keir Starmer and Morgan McSweeney found out.

If Britain continues under FPTP, then this governing chaos will deepen, and the only beneficiaries will be anti-democratic extremists.

But now there is a golden chance to change all this. Next Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament for its final stages. An amendment has been tabled to set up a national commission to look at which system of proportional representation (PR), which does match votes to seats, would best suit our country. It has huge backing in the Commons, in the Labour party and among the public. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is also a longstanding supporter of electoral reform. The political conditions have never been more favourable to begin making changes to the voting system. What could possibly go wrong?

This: a minority but powerful view within the upper reaches of the Labour party, the cabinet and the party bureaucracy is vehemently opposed to PR and the plural politics of cooperation it demands. According to this tribal view, only Labour, governing alone, can represent the interests of “their voters”. And so it is preferable to lose all power than to share it. Labour winning – however tiny its share of the vote – is more important than democracy working. At best, those with this view may calculate whether PR or FPTP delivers the most Labour MPs, equating self-interest with the national interest.

But all their paternalistic calculations miss the very big point: democracy should not be designed around what is best for Labour – or any party – but around what works best for the country.

Labour’s rearguard reactionaries will try to block the idea of a national commission, water it down or kick it bureaucratically into touch. They will say only the cost of living matters, and that no one brings up PR on the doorstep. But it is precisely our rotten voting system that denies the changes people want, because it prioritises the cautious views of a few swing voters in a few swing seats and impels Labour to pander to them.

The game is over for this old top-down, command-and-control politics. The myth of strong government from FPTP is dead. It is time for change, to do what Willy Brandt, the fabled leader of the German Social Democrats, implored the left to do in 1969, and “dare more democracy”. That means finally embracing multiparty government, and ensuring everyone’s vote is counted equally: it is the only way to end the cycle of chaos.
