Ayyoub Bouaddi: maths student, chess fan and Manchester City’s new Rodri

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 14:00:15 GMT

The £85m midfielder passed his exams a year early, is studying for a degree and is ready to tackle Premier League learning curve

“He’s like a computer,” the former Lille head of academy recruitment, Mathieu Frison, says of the €100m (£85.7m) Manchester City recruit Ayyoub Bouaddi. “You teach him something, he learns it and can do it immediately.” Bouaddi has the mountainous challenge at his new club of replacing the world’s best central midfielder. It would be difficult for anyone but at 18 it feels monumental, although those who know the Morocco international best would not bet against him.

Bouaddi has known only Lille and Ligue 1 but is entering one of the biggest clubs in the world where a season without a trophy is deemed a failure. For someone so young, however, he has plenty of experience. He made his European debut three days after his 16th birthday and has played three full seasons in the first team, culminating in a place at the World Cup this summer.

At 13, Lille beat off competition from France’s elite to sign Bouaddi, after showing his parents the pathway he could follow to the first team. There was never lengthy discussion over money, just what would be best for a boy who wanted to reach the highest level. Lille’s track record is impressive, the club bringing through Bouaddi’s soon-to-be Premier League rivals Carlos Baleba and Leny Yoro, among others, in recent times.

Frison visited the Bouaddi family in Creil, an hour north of Paris, to explain why a move to Lille would be beneficial after scouts spotted Bouaddi playing for his home town team in a tournament. “He was not here at the beginning of the meeting with his parents, and he came in the house with the ball on a string,” Frison recalls. “He did a very good trick; he always had this ball in his hand and he always played in his house, so he was already very talented technically.”

City have faith in him, although plenty of the expenditure is based on promise rather than a finished article. He is not someone who creates highlight reels, but does the dirty work and plays for the team. Others may have sought someone with more miles in their legs, but Enzo Maresca is rebuilding a midfield for the long term after Rodri’s departure for Barcelona and with a £52m deal agreed for Nico González to join Newcastle. The 23-year-old Elliot Anderson arrived from Nottingham Forest as the first cog in the machine, and Enzo Fernández is also wanted by his former manager at Chelsea.

Bouaddi, the only boy of four siblings, passed all his exams a year early, is studying for a mathematics degree remotely and speaks English. He is a deep thinker, someone able to cut out the distractions at home and on the pitch. “On the bus, while everyone is watching YouTube videos or listening to music, he will play chess for one or two hours,” Frison says. “In the evening when all the players played Fifa or were on their phones, he studied mathematics, physics, science. His parents didn’t need to push him to do this – he wanted to learn.”

Bouaddi represented the country of his birth, France, from under-16 to under-21 and is regarded as a huge loss for Les Bleus. “Bouaddi, for me, is one of the smartest players I’ve known in my coaching career,” says the former France under-18 coach Landry Chauvin, who had Bouaddi in his squad for the Lafarge tournament in Limoges in 2024. “He reminds me a lot of Yoann Gourcuff, who I saw in Rennes a few years ago. As soon as the tournament was over, I told Les Espoirs [France’s Under-21s] that he should have nothing more to do with me, that he had to continue to progress and go above and beyond.”

Rodri has won everything worth winning over the past decade while Bouaddi was growing up. Emulating the Spaniard will not be straightforward for a player who is a long way from being fully developed. “When Maresca asks him to do something tactically, he knows that 100% Ayyoub will take the best position for the team,” Frison says.

“He will respect the game model with intensity, even when he is tired; he will respect the process. Everyone wants a player who can make the difference individually because they can help you to win the game but you need reliable players who you can trust 100% during 60 games of the season. And Ayyoub, he’s this kind of player.”

Bouaddi has consistently mixed with – and surpassed – older players, quickly improving as he rapidly went through each step to the top. He was 16 when he featured for Chauvin’s France Under-18s and on his 17th birthday he faced Real Madrid in the Champions League, playing 90 minutes in a 1-0 win against Jude Bellingham et al.

“A very intelligent boy who adapts quickly, capable of playing in every position in the middle, capable of evolving in a changing environment, permanently working hard, but also always with his head held high,” Chauvin says. “He has the ability to scan the actions very quickly, to take the information before the others. Very comfortable technically, he always has the right position on the field. And on top of that, he’s a boy who’s charming in everyday life; very respectful, very well educated, who knows all the rules.

“The man who hides behind the footballer is simply a very beautiful person. Every time I went to Lille, I would send him a little text, and immediately he came to greet me, even though he was already a pro. Many in his place would have snubbed the under-18 coach, but not Ayyoub.”

Nectar Classic memory foam mattress review: an outstanding budget buy

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 14:00:14 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

With a genuinely impressive lifetime guarantee, Nectar’s mattress outperforms pricier rivals for comfort and motion isolation

The best mattresses, tested

Memory foam has been called the Marmite of the bed industry. Nice soundbite, but I think it’s more like butter – because many mattresses now include a “comfort layer” of this squishy material to make them more palatable. You wouldn’t eat a whole block of butter, though, and you probably wouldn’t want to sleep on a mattress made entirely from memory foam. Too much squish, too little support.

The Nectar Classic memory foam, like so many of the best foam and hybrid (foam and springs) mattresses, tempers the marshmallowy feel of true memory foam by sandwiching it between other types of foam, namely breathable polyfoam and dense support foam. As I discovered when testing it, this creates a lovely balance of comfort and firmness that feels more like a hybrid mattress, only without the bounce.

At £449 for a double, the Nectar Classic memory foam is also excellent value, especially as it comes with a lifetime guarantee that genuinely deserves to be called “industry leading”. Here, I tear myself away from its cosy embrace to reveal why I loved it, despite wanting a fight with its washing label.

I was sent a double-size Nectar Classic memory foam mattress in May, just as temperatures first punched past the 30C mark. Once I’d given the mattress a couple of days to expand to its full size and firmness, my family testing panel came over to rate it out of 10 for comfort, aesthetics and other subjective factors. They also helped me run lab-style experiments with heat pads, weights and wobbly cups of water to measure its sinkage, motion isolation, heat retention and edge support. Here’s more on our mattress-testing shenanigans – cats, bottoms and all.

My husband, Alan, and I slept on the Nectar for six weeks in June and July, after positioning it on a slatted Ikea base and covering it with a mattress protector and cotton bedding. It was the worst of times for sleeping. The room temperature occasionally dropped below 28C with the help of an electric fan, but for the most part it hovered around 32C. The fact that we managed to sleep on the Nectar, rather than just lie on it, shows how well it performed on temperature control.

Delivery, sustainability and manoeuvrability are vital considerations every time I test a mattress. Quick delivery, plenty of text updates, helpful handlers and recyclable packaging are big green flags. Factors such as UK manufacture, low-carbon processes and mattress recycling schemes help boost the otherwise low sustainability ranking of foam.

Then there’s price. Instead of looking for cheapness per se, I want value for money and durability, especially from a product that’s as difficult to dispose of as a memory foam mattress.

The Classic memory foam is Nectar’s most popular mattress, according to the brand, and part of a range that also includes another all-foam mattress (the Premier), two foam-and-spring hybrid mattresses, and a kids’ mattress. The Classic memory foam is the most affordable of Nectar’s adult mattresses: £199 for a single, rising to £649 for a super-king. The double I tested costs £449. That’s cheaper than the Tempur Ease – another all-foam mattress with a feel and performance similar to the Nectar.

The Nectar Classic isn’t just a massive chunk of high-viscosity memory foam. As with most modern foam mattresses, it combines layers of foam of different densities. Immediately below the fabric cover is a top layer of breathable polyfoam to help regulate body temperature and add a little bounce, followed by a thick middle layer of memory foam for cushioning, then a base layer of dense foam for support and durability.

Nectar rates the mattress as “6.5 out of 10 (medium-firm)”, but it feels firmer than that when you first sleep on it. My testing panel gave it an average 8/10, and then, after Alan and I had slept on it for a month, we rated it 7/10 (where 10 is firmest). This isn’t a fault: all foam mattresses soften after being slept on, then settle after a while to their intended tension level.

The fabric sleep surface is made from synthetic fabric (9.5% low-density polyethylene and 90.5% polyester), while the bottom cover is 100% polyester. Nectar says the fabric is woven with “cooling fibres” and describes it as “menopause-friendly”, explaining that it “wicks heat away and encourages airflow”.

The Nectar’s cover isn’t removable, despite having a giant zip that you can unzip all the way round to, yes, remove the cover (I agree, it makes no sense). When I unzipped it, partly to investigate the layers inside, I found a washing label that warned: “non-removable cover”, “do not wash”, “do not dry clean” and “zip for manufacturing use only”. So while you can remove the cover, you’re not supposed to.

Nectar’s warranty doesn’t explicitly discuss this, but I’d play it safe and keep that zip zipped. While the headline warranty term is “forever”, which genuinely beats any other mattress guarantee I’ve seen (besides DreamCloud, which shares a parent company with Nectar), limitations include any use “in violation of instructions” – such as removing the cover. If the mattress is defective within 10 years, you’ll get a replacement. From year 11, Nectar will completely repair and re-cover it.

Type: memory foamMaterials: polyurethane foam filling; polyester and polyethylene coverFirmness: advertised as medium-firm; panel rated as 8/10 after two days, then we rated as 7/10 after six weeksDepth: 25cmCover: do not removeTurn or rotate: “rotate regularly”, according to label; rotate “every few months”, according to the Nectar blogTrial: 365 nightsWarranty: forever, with limitationsOld mattress recycling: £60Sustainability credentials: mattresses are made in the UK using CertiPur- and Oeko-Tex-certified foam; Nectar works with ClimatePartner to reduce environmental footprint; returned mattresses are donated to the British Heart Foundation

Nectar mattresses are shrink-wrapped into boxes and delivered by BJS Home Delivery, and the service was excellent in my experience. BJS kept me updated via text and WhatsApp, sending me a three-hour window on the day before delivery, and including a tracking link that proved useful and accurate.

The two delivery drivers asked if I wanted them to carry the box upstairs and even remove the packaging, but I was happy for them to leave it in the hallway. At 32kg for a double, the Nectar Classic is one of the lighter mattresses I’ve tested, and the box was small enough for me to lug upstairs by myself – a rare treat in my life as a mattress reviewer.

The first thing I loved was how blissfully easy this mattress was to carry up the stairs and unpack. I use double-size mattresses in my tests for the Filter because a king-size pocket-sprung mattress would get stuck in our narrow, angled stairwell. But the Nectar Classic memory foam is so light and tightly rolled that even a super-king would have made it upstairs easily. Given the affordability and manoeuvrability of the Nectar Classic, I’d recommend buying the largest size your bedroom has space for.

After giving the mattress a couple of days to expand, we invited our family over for their verdict. My sister Maeve, who identifies as a memory-foam sceptic, declared herself “really surprised” by how firm and breathable it felt. Her husband, Ben, is easier to please (any bed works, as long as he can sleep in it immediately), but agreed: “this is better than the other foam mattresses [we’ve tested]. I can even sit on the edge of this one without sinking.”

When settling in for the sleep test, Alan and I also loved how flat, supportive and airy the mattress was. This is largely because the Nectar’s top layer is much less mouldable than the Tempur Pro Plus SmartCool and the Panda bamboo mattress topper. The middle layer is more “sinky” and helps with pressure relief, but its top layer springs back more quickly than pure memory foam when you press it, which makes it feel less cloying.

I slept much better on the Nectar than I’d expected to, given the heat of June and July. Over the weeks, it softened slightly to cushion my pressure points, but it never softened too much. When we ran our sinkage tests in the first week, the sleep surface sank 2cm under 7.5kg of weights. By the end of week four, it sank 2.7cm – less than the Simba Hybrid Pro. I was still measuring 2.7cm in week six, which suggests the softening had settled.

The Nectar Classic’s motion isolation is outstanding, as is often the case with foam. While the “non-sinky” upper layer made it easy to turn in bed, the lower layer of adaptive foam seemed to absorb our movements so we never disturbed each other while fidgeting.

The Nectar was more comfortable in the heatwave than I’d expected from a foam mattress with a polyester cover. That’s damning with faint praise, though. It only performed moderately well on temperature control, and I suspect that my electric fan, cotton bedsheets and bamboo duvet (the summer edition of the Panda Cloud, which topped my best duvets test) did a lot of heavy lifting to help me sleep.

In my heat-retention test, the Nectar’s surface took marginally longer to fall back to ambient room temperature than Panda’s memory foam mattress topper, which I recently tested under similar balmy conditions. That said, I never experienced night sweats on the Nectar, unlike the Otty Bamboo topper, which I had to drag off our bed at 4am.

The slight softening of the mattress over our weeks of sleeping was expected given its foam composition, but it never sagged. If you sleep on your back or your front, however, it may become too soft for you. If, on the other hand, you crave the sink-in pressure relief of memory foam, it may feel too firm. There’s also no bounce, so this probably won’t be your first choice if you love a springy bed.

Foam and hybrid mattresses usually have fabric covers that you can unzip to wash in the machine, but the Nectar doesn’t (remember, ignore the zip!). This helps to keep its price down because there’s no inner lining to protect the foam when the cover is off. However, it does mean that you have to buy a mattress protector and use it diligently to keep the mattress in good condition, especially during its one-year trial period.

Memory foam (viscoelastic polyurethane foam) is one of the least sustainable materials used in furnishings. It’s made using petroleum-derived chemicals including polyols and diisocyanates, and emits volatile organic compounds (VOCs) when removed from its shrink-wrapping at home. That’s what the “off-gassing” smell is.

Nectar is working to limit the damage, though. It claims it has offset 43m kilograms of carbon to date, and has enlisted the help of ClimatePartner to cut its footprint rather than just offset it. Among its plans are a switch away from polyurethane foam to a “low-emission alternative”, and “updates on plastic packaging”. Meanwhile, all its foam is CertiPur and Oeko-Tex certified, and its mattresses are made in Manchester and delivered in FSC-certified cardboard.

Nectar charges £60 to collect your old mattress when you buy a new one from the company. Where a mattress can’t be resold, it’s donated to the British Heart Foundation (BHF). Nectar says this scheme has raised more than £1.2m for the BHF. Nectar’s lifetime warranty is also worth mentioning here because it will help you avoid having to dispose of your mattress for many years.

The Nectar Classic memory foam mattress is an outstanding buy. It’s one of the lightest and easiest-to-manoeuvre mattresses I’ve tested, beaten only by the budget Ikea Valevåg. This makes it an excellent choice for anyone moving house or setting up home – or indeed, anyone blessed with a tight stairwell like mine.

It’s easy to sleep on, too. Side sleepers may initially find it too firm, but it adapts to cushion your pressure points and strike a lovely balance of comfort and support. Despite testing this mattress in a heatwave, I never woke up at 4am in a pool of sweat and misery, as I have with a few other memory foam products.

I wouldn’t call it a “cooling” mattress, though. If overheating is a problem for you, I’d recommend a sprung or hybrid mattress instead. Sprung mattresses also tend to be a more sustainable choice.

Those are the main reasons I gave this mattress four stars rather than five, although I’d give it four and a half if I could. It feels durable enough to last for many years, and its generous warranty backs this up.

The Nectar is no Marmite mattress. You may love it, but you’re highly unlikely to hate it. It’ll appeal to a wide range of people, including side sleepers, back sleepers and couples, and it’s well worth its price.

The firm-but-cosy feel of the Nectar Classic reminded me more of the brilliant Otty than any other mattress. The Nectar is cheaper, though (the Otty costs £599.99 for a double; currently £540 with the code FILTER10), and lighter, so it’s easier to move around. Why, then, did I give the Otty five stars, and the Nectar only four? The Otty, which contains springs as well as layers of foam, dissipated heat more quickly in my tests than the Nectar. It also felt more instantly comfortable, whereas the Nectar needed a couple of weeks to develop a bit of “give” under my pressure points. Its lower proportion of foam gives it the edge on sustainability, too. It won’t shout at you for removing and washing its cover, either.

Read our full Otty Original Hybrid mattress review

The Tempur Ease doesn’t hide its memory foam layer in the middle like the Nectar, but puts it immediately under the fabric cover (which you can unzip to wash, hooray). The overall effect is still reassuringly supportive, but it feels more yielding and may be a better choice for side sleepers. If you crave a marshmallowy memory foam surface, though – and can afford the investment – I’d recommend the medium edition of Tempur’s Pro SmartCool mattress. I found it too soft, but it makes you feel fully suspended in your bed and is fantastic for pain relief.

I had some of the best sleeps of my life on the Simba Hybrid Pro. The foam layers give it fantastic motion isolation and a sumptuous feel. It softened quite a lot over my months of testing, though, and it’s heavier than the Nectar. Its price is weighty, too, at £1,299 for a double at RRP (£909.30 at the time of writing in the brand’s bank holiday sale).

Stephen Libby on fashion: I’m on a mission to revive the jumpsuit – they’re practical and stylish

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 13:00:14 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

The 70s was a golden era for the jumpsuit, but I’m happy they’re back, thanks to Harry Styles, Benson Boone and – of course – me

Since appearing on The Traitors, I’ve become synonymous with jumpsuits. In fact, I’ve been required to wear one at every public appearance I have made since it aired, despite only wearing two on the show. That’s the power of the jumpsuit, I guess.

When I was packing for the show, I wasn’t even sure I would bring them – and not everyone watching liked them. Lots of people did, but I got messages saying: “What the hell is he wearing?”. The memes were also phenomenal. My favourite was my head on John Travolta’s body in a still from Saturday Night Fever.

I now own five jumpsuits – which is probably five more than almost any other man – and they all tend to be quite 70s in style. This was a golden period for the men’s jumpsuit, when David Bowie and Elton John wore them, and they really became a part of popular culture. They’ve since faded into obscurity and now the only men we see wearing them are those who are very comfortable with their sexuality, such as Benson Boone and Harry Styles.

You can see echoes of the 70s in some modern men’s clothes, whether it’s a geometric pattern or a wide lapel, but jumpsuits seem to be a bridge too far for most people. I love them because they’re so practical. I take quite a while to get ready at the best of times, and they are a whole outfit in one. As for going to the loo, it’s easier than with trousers because there’s no button, just a zip.

I bought my first jumpsuit six years ago. It was from a brand called Palomo Spain, cost about £300 and I saved up for 18 months to buy it. It’s orange and blue with short sleeves, and one of the ones I wore on TV. The moment I wore it out of the house, that was it: it became the gateway drug to my jumpsuit era. People have referred to it as a boilersuit, but I would never get under the bonnet of a car wearing that beautiful garment.

The next one I bought was also Palomo Spain. It was black and white and very chic. You might recognise it from the finale of Traitors – though I very nearly didn’t wear that either. I bought it a while before filming started, and then discovered Harry Styles had worn the same one on tour. Nothing against Harry, but I pride myself on trying to be as unique as possible, so I’d already earmarked a beautiful micro-checked 70s suit for the finale. The problem was, when I put it on, we discovered the print was causing the camera to strobe. The only thing I hadn’t worn was the jumpsuit, so I ended up wearing that. And of course, I became “Stephen from Traitors in the jumpsuits”.

A good jumpsuit can really elongate your body. The trick is making sure the waist sits where the waist of your trousers would sit. For me, that’s quite high up, but you can get things altered to what works for you. Unlike a lot of menswear, the jumpsuit is the main event, so you don’t need to accessorise much. I’d probably wear a loafer, or a Cuban heel – just not trainers. Jumpsuits aren’t really casual items of clothing so trainers would just look a bit off.

I’ve not seen many affordable jumpsuit options for men, who tend to favour overalls or boilersuits (as far as I’m concerned, these are different garments with a slouchy fit or a drop crotch). My tip is to buy a women’s one and just get it altered. Reiss do some fantastic denim jumpsuits which you can get in a longer leg, as do Me+Em. Other than that, it’s vintage all the way.

I’m always on the hunt for the perfect jumpsuit. I remember seeing a photo of David Bowie leaving Studio 54 wearing one by Willie Brown. It’s not a classic 70s style, and is in fact quite loose, but I said to myself: “ I need to own something like this in my lifetime.” I still haven’t found the exact one, but I’m about to bid on a purple disco number from the 1970s. Wish me luck!

‘I catch the signs a lot earlier now’: Amanda Anisimova on burnout and bouncing back

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 13:00:13 GMT

World No 10 is one of the best players yet to win a major and heads to Flushing Meadows in fine form after learning to embrace being uncomfortable

Amanda Anisimova can see the signs now. It is just over three years since the American announced she would be taking an indefinite break for mental health reasons. A brilliant junior, she was a semi-finalist at the French Open in 2019 and seemingly destined for the top, only for her world to be rocked by the sudden death of her father, Konstantin, a few months later. Struggling for motivation and burned out, in May 2023, she revealed she would be stepping away from the sport.

It turned out to be the best decision she ever made. “I learned how important it is to have a great balance on and off the court,” Anisimova says in an interview from New York, ahead of the US Open, where she will try to go one better than last year and win her first grand slam title.

“That’s something that I used to not prioritise so much: how to recharge myself and take time for myself, prioritise my wellbeing off the court. In the past, it was really just a lot of tennis and I didn’t really know how to incorporate those small breaks for myself. I think that’s a big reason why I reached such a breaking point and needed to take that time away from the sport.”

Three years on, Anisimova is better able to feel when things are becoming too much. For a top tennis player, with a tour that’s an 11-month grind, there are not many obvious opportunities for lengthy breaks, but Anisimova finds time for herself. If she is not feeling it on the practice or match court, she takes herself away.

“I feel like I’ve become so much more self-aware now of when I’m anticipating or feeling like I’m reaching that point where I don’t feel as excited or as motivated,” she says. “Those signs are much more alarming to me now, and I catch them a lot earlier than I did before.

“Before, sometimes I felt like that was a normal thing, but now I know that’s not a normal thing to experience or go through. At least not to let it keep happening. It’s obviously normal to get tired or burnt out, and we all have days where we don’t feel like doing the things we need to do. It’s about how to manage that and navigate that. I think that’s been the biggest thing that I’ve learned, and that’s helped me tremendously as an athlete.”

Anisimova finished 2025 at No 4 in the rankings, a remarkable achievement, not least because of what happened to her at Wimbledon. After beating Aryna Sabalenka in the semi-finals with a brilliant performance, she crumbled in her first major final, frozen with fear, her feet stuck, her racket arm feeling like it weighed a ton. The result was a 6-0, 6-0 thumping by a ruthless Iga Swiatek and an unwanted place in the history books as the first woman to not win a game in a Wimbledon final in more than a century.

Many players would never have recovered from the experience but Anisimova’s time away has helped her to see the bigger picture. As painful as the day was, reaching a first grand slam final was a huge milestone. “I try to have a lot of perspective, and I think that really grounds me in a lot of situations,” says Anisimova, who was speaking as an ambassador for Pure Leaf Iced Tea.

“When I take maybe 10 minutes for myself to just kind of reset and think about what it is I’m going through and have that perspective in mind, then I think that really helps me sometimes. And it’s not something that I really had when I was 20, 21.”

after newsletter promotion

Her resilience is remarkable. She took revenge on Swiatek at the US Open to reach a second consecutive major final and pushed Sabalenka hard in the title decider. She won her fourth WTA Tour title in China and ended 2025 by making the last four at the WTA Finals. After hitting No 3 in January, a wrist injury stopped her momentum but she looks back on form, a quarter-final run in Cincinnati setting her up nicely for the US Open, playing at home in a tournament and on a surface she loves. “I feel like I found some rhythm on the court again,” she says. “I’m looking forward to the US Open. Feeling good. It’s my favourite time of the year by far.”

With perhaps the best backhand on Tour, Anisimova has the firepower required of a major champion. Her timing could be very good, too, with many of the leading contenders for the US Open looking vulnerable, including defending champion Sabalenka, whose form has dipped in recent months. Coco Gauff won in Cincinnati but there is an opportunity for someone to come through. One of the best players yet to win a major, there is pressure on Anisimova to deliver, but she enjoys pushing herself.

“I have that eagerness and that motivation to achieve my dreams and win a grand slam one day,” she said. “A lot of the things that it takes to get there, it’s not as pretty or as glamorous as people think. But I also love a challenge, and that’s why I am where I am today. I’m a pro athlete, and you don’t get to the place where you are without being uncomfortable. I think it’s just embracing that. You’re going to be uncomfortable 90% of the time, but I’m so driven by my goals, so that definitely makes it easier and more enjoyable for me.

“It’s always been a dream to win a grand slam. You don’t really think about your dream as winning a [WTA] 1,000. It’s always the biggest thing you can win, whether it’s a grand slam or the Olympics, which both are huge dreams of athletes. For me, it was always the US Open. I think there’s just something about winning a grand slam that completes a tennis player’s life.”

Goodbye, Dolly Parton: a gay icon whose appeal reached across age, class and politics, and into the Maga heartlands

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 12:33:55 GMT

Straight women loved her, so did Eminem. Even Donald Trump found something nice to say. Her allure had no boundaries and was truly unique

I was at the National Theatre in London on Tuesday night, at a production of Pride, which tells the story of the unlikely alliance between gay activists and Welsh miners during the 1984 miners’ strike, when news broke of Dolly Parton’s death. Well. Against the sadness, one couldn’t help smiling. At a very gay production, attended by a majority gay audience, I half expected them to stop the show or call out a team from St John Ambulance bearing stretchers. In the script for Pride, references to Judy Garland and Ethel Merman serve as shorthand for gay sensibilities, but it could just as easily have been Dolly Parton. The queen of country and crossover pop was beloved by so many communities – many antagonistic to each other – but it was perhaps her gay fans who claimed her most vociferously and publicly.

When we got home my friends and I danced around to 9 to 5, and on Wednesday morning it was Here You Come, Again (“looking better than a body has a right to” – oh, Dolly) on a loop, along with her 1971 hit Coat of Many Colors.

Parton was, in some ways, an unlikely gay icon. She was studiously neutral on a great many subjects, including politics, and while she could be funny and waspish, the person she most often poked fun at was herself. In my colleague Alexis Petridis’s lovely tribute, he mentions Parton’s 1977 encounter with Barbara Walters – a woman so rich in spite and Chanel suits as to win her her own following in corners of the gay community. She asked Dolly: “Do you ever feel that you’re a joke?” One was struck by Parton’s smiling response – “I’m sure of myself as a person. I’m sure of my talent” – relative to how Katharine Hepburn, a gay icon with a more traditional way of handling things, responded to similar nastiness from Walters. When the journalist asked her, “Do you ever wear a skirt?”, Hepburn clapped back: “I have one. I’ll wear it to your funeral.” In a million years, Parton wouldn’t have been rude like that.

All of which, you might think – and despite the bouffant hair and rhinestone wardrobe – might have lessened her appeal to gay audiences. But Parton had something else. The voice, of course, but to me it was also a question of sincerity. She meant it: every rhinestone, every teased, backcombed strand of hair in the blowout. She could joke about her image with the best of them, but we all knew that when it came down to it, Parton was deadly serious about the way she looked. There is a hard, gleaming gemstone at the core of camp culture that isn’t funny at all. It exists in absolute earnest, a private space of joy and pain and beauty undiluted by judgment. It’s hard to say precisely how one knows the difference between the endless fake, gay-baiting uses to which this tone is put and the real thing, but one does. Gay rights was one of the few issues on which Parton didn’t stay neutral – she threw the Bible at homophobes, asking them who they thought they were to pass judgment – but it wasn’t that. You just knew.

And yet if there’s another thing we knew about Dolly Parton, it was her genius to cross every barrier of age, sexuality, race and politics. In a recent poll conducted by the University of Massachusetts Lowell, Parton was the only person in the survey to win higher than a 50% approval rating from Democrats, Republicans and independents. She crossed class barriers, too. While the Democratic Socialists of America praised Parton for being “a hero of the working class”, the now-billionaire president, Donald Trump, issued possibly the most positive statement he has ever made about another human being, saying of Parton: “There has never been anyone like her, and never will.”

Eminem posted a tribute. Straight women loved her, including one of my aunts, who when she went platinum blond in her 60s was fond of quoting Parton’s famous line – “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap” – by way of justification. Parton owned it all, and was god-level smart and as kind as they come, which may have been at the root of how she pulled off the seemingly impossible feat of being genuinely adored by all. When Trump ordered the nation’s flags to be lowered, one marvelled again at her unique status as someone as beloved in rural Kentucky as she was in Hell’s Kitchen.

On Wednesday morning, my friends and I only had eyes for the gay stuff, including a statement released by Jane Fonda, with whom she starred, alongside Lily Tomlin – what a triumvirate – in the 1980 film 9 to 5. Fonda said: “To her gay and trans fans, I want you to know that she loved you.” Meanwhile Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, who was her head of security, as was his father, Larry, before him, issued a video statement on behalf of the family. “Dolly has lived in the light,” he said, movingly. When Bryan said: “May god bless you all, she will always love you,” I had my biggest wobble.

To quote another gay icon, Barbra Streisand: it’s the laughter we’ll remember. At the production of Pride on Tuesday night, my friend told me his Dolly story. I hope it’s alright to mention this; I can’t help but think Dolly would’ve enjoyed it. He was at a (gay) wedding deep in rural Tennessee a few years ago and thought he’d take a quick look at Grindr, the gay hook-up app. As expected, in that grimly traditional part of the US, it was an absolute gay desert, except for a bizarre cluster in a single spot about 40 miles down the road. Surprised, my friend glanced at the map and burst out laughing. Of course: Dollywood. What a gift she was to all of us – but to some of us, perhaps, more than others. Thank you, Dolly, for everything. God, we’ll miss you.

The great Snowdon queue-skipping row – is it really OK to jump the line if you’re not taking a selfie?

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 11:20:01 GMT

The crowds at the top of Yr Wyddfa, the highest mountain in Wales, are now so huge that seasoned hikers and climbers are simply walking past them. Is everyone just making a mountain out of a molehill?

Name: The Snowdon queue.

Age: A decade and a half, give or take.

Appearance: Frustratingly long.

This isn’t new. You’re right. The press has been reporting on the queue to reach the summit of Yr Wyddfa in north Wales (known in English as Snowdon) since 2013.

I have never understood that. Really? Yr Wyddfa is an important national landmark, in one of the most beautiful parts of the UK. It’s bound to attract crowds – so people should expect to queue!

British people are so weird … It isn’t just British people. In 2019, people queued for so long to reach the summit of Mount Everest that some of them actually died. If you want to climb a mountain in 2026, expect to join a line.

You still haven’t explained why this is suddenly newsworthy. No, I haven’t, and for good reason. What I’m about to tell you will shake you to your very core. You might want to brace yourself.

This sounds awful. It’s worse than awful. Get this: people have started skipping the queue.

WHAAAT?! I know, and I’m sorry. People just aren’t having it any more. Social media has been flooded with Yr Wyddfa queue jumpers. “Imagine queueing on a mountain. No chance,” a climber huffs in one video, as he’s heckled by his more patient compatriots.

And it’s not a terrible one-off? If only. Another queue jumper posted a video, captioned: “Won’t catch me hiking for two hours to spend 30 minutes queueing at the top.”

This is the least British thing I have ever heard. Put yourself in their position, though. You’ve spent hours literally climbing a mountain, but then you have to stop near the top so a long line of bozos can take selfies at the peak to prove they made it. What would you do in that situation?

I would queue up, because I understand that some things are sacred. Yes, actually, I would, too. Skipping a queue is the least British thing of all time. It’s like insulting Paddington Bear.

Someone needs to be blamed for this. I mean, we could blame the rampant culture of overtourism that sent all these people there in the first place. About 600,000 people reach Yr Wyddfa’s summit every year, each bringing litter, traffic and vegetation erosion with them. Maybe some of them could go elsewhere?

No, that’s not it. Maybe, then, we could blame social media for increasing the time spent at the peak? If everyone was banned from taking a selfie at the top, the lines would almost certainly speed up a bit.

Can’t we just blame the queue jumpers? Oh God, yes, let’s just do that. Who do they think they are, disrespecting national etiquette like this?

Do say: “Queue jumpers are the scourge of Yr Wyddfa.”

Don’t say: “But maybe the problem has … peaked?”

Uefa to lift boycott threat after Fifa promises no World Cup sale repeat

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 11:16:27 GMT

Uefa has received guarantees after ill-fated Infantino plan

European sides will go to under-20 Women’s World Cup

Uefa is to drop its threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after receiving concrete guarantees that the global governing body will never attempt a repeat of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

European teams have been cleared for participation in the upcoming Under-20 Women’s World Cup, along with subsequent tournaments, after Fifa provided the binding assurances that no equivalent of its president’s ill-fated scheme will be put on the table.

Uefa had threatened the ­boycott after Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal was revealed and ­doubled down after it was ­withdrawn, saying the condition that “such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again” had not been met.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Despite exchanging barbs in ­public, Uefa and Fifa are understood to have been having private ­discussions over the terms of ­removing the ­boycott threat for several weeks, with the European governing body finally ­getting the reassurances it required.

When Fifa confirmed its decision to abandon FFE four days after it became public it neglected to pledge that a similar privatisation plan would not be repeated, but it has now done so in private correspondence.

The decision to drop the boycott allows England, who named their squad for the under-20 tournament last week, to travel to Poland in time for the opening game against Canada on 5 September. France and Spain had also listed their travelling party in anticipation that the boycott threat would be lifted. Portugal, Italy and the host nation are the other European countries due to compete.

Fifa welcomed the end of the boycott , saying: “Fifa is pleased that all qualified teams ‌will be participating in the upcoming Fifa Under-20 Women’s World Cup. Fifa strongly believes that football has the power to unite, even in challenging circumstances, and looks forward to welcoming all teams and players to Poland.”

The boycott is yet to be publicly dropped by Uefa, whose executive committee and federation chiefs meet in Monte Carlo on Thursday. The 55 heads of Uefa’s member associations will convene before the Champions League draw during what is traditionally a significant few days in the European football calendar.

Uefa’s position that Infantino must be replaced has not changed and further steps regarding its stance towards the Fifa leadership will also be discussed at the meeting.

Italy’s football federation (FIGC) on Wednesday became the latest to publicly withdraw support for Infantino. “This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC’s position … regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the Fifa president concerning the governance and development of international competitions,” it said.

There will be relief in some quarters that younger players, in particular, will not become embroiled in the volatile battle for football’s future. But the fact that Fifa has been forced to mitigate for its president’s actions is another humiliation for a persistently scandal-hit organisation.

Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 11:00:12 GMT

The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected

A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?

Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.

Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.

It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox.

It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US.

There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.

The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk.

In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.

“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.

“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.

The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.

The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.

If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.

Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.

“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.”

However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”

Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”

Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.

The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.

Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”

A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.

An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.

While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.

“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”

This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 11:00:10 GMT

They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’

The midterm elections are already upon us, and every Democrat and independent running against a Republican should ask voters the question Ronald Reagan asked on 28 October 1980, at the end of his televised debate against Jimmy Carter: “Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?”

Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”

Start with his tariffs, which are costing every American household an average of $1,100 annually, according to the Yale Budget Lab. (If you don’t trust Yale, the conservative Tax Foundation estimated last year’s tab to be $1,000 a household.)

Even cleaning supplies and toilet paper are up at least 5%. Household furnishings, up at least 8%. Clothing, up at least 14%. Trump’s tariffs have also increased the costs of big-ticket items such as cars and made it more expensive to build new homes.

Other studies find that the tariffs have added as much as 0.7 and 0.5 percentage points to the consumer price index and the personal consumption expenditures price index, respectively.

Then there’s Trump’s war in Iran, which is driving up energy and food prices, as oil tankers remain stranded in the strait of Hormuz.

The war is costing more at the gas pump – about $670 more a household since the war began. Americans face what the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers describe as “a worsening utility debt crisis”. The groups wrote in an analysis published last month:

Energy bills have increased three times faster than the rate of inflation while Trump has been president. The national average monthly utility bill reached $280 in early 2026, a 12% increase since the end of 2024, just before the second Trump administration took office.

What’s the Republican response to soaring energy utility prices? Eliminate billions in clean energy subsidies and tilt the scales toward costlier, dirtier fossil fuels.

Also driving up the cost of electricity are AI datacenters. They’re also using up huge amounts of water and creating noise pollution. And who’s been pushing these datacenters? Trump and, before recent backlash, many Republicans.

Trump’s war and the blockage of the strait are also causing fertilizer shortages, which are sending food prices upward. Millions of Americans are now struggling to afford groceries.

Meanwhile, Trump’s huge tax cuts – which mostly benefited big corporations and the super-wealthy – are being paid for, in part, by Republican cuts to Medicaid and Medicare.

Trump announced last month that he is ending Medicare subsidies that have kept drug prices low for seniors; Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act have deprived millions of Americans of health insurance.

Hell, even Trump’s executive order to divide the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine into three shots instead of one is adding burdens to the typical American family.

As the Republican senator Bill Cassidy said on ABC’s This Week: “This is why the president’s poll numbers are down, because you’ve lost sight of affordability for the parent. You’ve lost sight of the convenience for the American family. You’ve lost sight of that which is driving higher costs in healthcare – for example, more doctor’s visits … for something which has no rationale in science.”

Trump’s obsession with gutting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has denied Americans billions in foregone rebates and settlements.

The regime spent $464m of taxpayer dollars in a no-bid contract for a special fleet of jets intended to deport immigrants. The planes have almost never been used.

On and on it goes.

Trump says the US economy is “doing unbelievably from the standpoint of Wall Street”.

Maybe, but most Americans live on Main Street and own few if any shares of stock. The richest 1% holds more than half of the value of stocks listed on US stock exchanges; the richest 10%, 92%. Even including retirement accounts, only 16% of adult Americans have assets exceeding $100,000.

The stock market boom reflects a boom in corporate profits. The pharmaceutical industry, big oil, and other sectors are posting banner earnings. Second quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are on pace to rise a remarkable 50% year over year, the highest growth rate since the second quarter of 2021.

But average working Americans are struggling to keep their heads above water.

Trump’s comments about the roaring stock market came the same day that new data showed US consumer sentiment dropped in August. Americans’ outlook on the country’s economic conditions have worsened among Republicans as well as among Democrats.

The July jobs report showed the US economy shedding 23,000 jobs, wage growth slowing, and the unemployment rate falling because more people left the workforce.

My humble advice to Democratic candidates in the midterms: don’t be distracted. Don’t take the bait and discuss socialism, “wokeism”, or anything else.

Just ask this simple question: are you better off now than you were before this presidency? And explain how badly Trump and congressional Republicans have shafted average working people.

You’re better off than you were before the start of this presidency only if you’re a major investor in the stock market, a top corporate executive or a beneficiary of Trump’s largesse to his billionaire backers.

But if you’re an average working American, you’re indubitably worse off. Hopefully, you’ll vote your economic interests on 3 November and deposit Trump’s congressional lapdogs into the dustbin of history.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich. substack. com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

Americans say they lose weight in Europe – and I think I know why

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 10:00:41 GMT

Is it because of differences in the flour that’s being consumed? Or something to do with the European approach to getting around?

It’s not just the mass shootings you have to watch out for in the US, it’s also the lettuce – a dodgy bit of iceberg could leave you sick with cyclosporiasis. And then there are the frozen blueberries, recently recalled because of a “reasonable probability” they could “cause serious adverse health consequences or even death”. And the alfalfa sprouts that may harbour salmonella. And the fruit bars that may be contaminated with glass. I could go on: there’s been a surge in foodborne illnesses in the US this year and food recalls have been getting a lot of attention.

Europe obviously isn’t immune to foodborne illnesses either. More than 200 people have become sick in the UK this summer and one person has died because of a salmonella outbreak tied to imported eggs. Still, Europe is widely seen as having far more robust regulations and food policies than the US. There’s endless anecdata online from Americans who claim that American bread and pasta makes them feel bloated and sick, but they can eat whatever they want in Europe and feel great.

Podcaster Joe Rogan, for example, has said pasta and bread “wreck” him in the US, but not in Italy. He cited US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr’s theory that heavily processed (“enriched flour”) in the US could be to blame. Social media is full of people with similar claims. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal published a piece called My Secret Diet is a Trip to Europe, showcasing Americans who dropped weight while eating their way across the continent.

I’m about as qualified to weigh in on this matter as RFK Jr, so here’s my personal hypothesis: for most of these Americans, I think it’s less about the food, and more about the fact that they are walking a lot more on their holidays than they do at home. People in the US look at me like I must be either indigent or deeply eccentric when I tell them I don’t have a car. Beyond a few cities, you can’t actually walk anywhere in the US because there are no pavements and the infrastructure is hostile to pedestrians. In the 1920s, the auto industry even lobbied for “jaywalking” laws to criminalise crossing the road and cast pedestrians as ridiculous simpletons. I’m no scientist, but I reckon my theory has legs.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Miley Cyrus, Taylor Swift and more pay tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘her legacy will be everlasting’

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 07:46:12 GMT

Lily Tomlin, Beyoncé, Céline Dion and Oprah Winfrey are among those remembering the queen of country after she died aged 80

Alexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless career that turned country music cliches inside out

Dolly Parton – a life in pictures

Dolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and more

Tributes have poured in for Dolly Parton, the country singer, songwriter and actor, after her death aged 80.

News of her death was shared by her nephew on social media. “Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus,” he said.

Earlier this year, Parton had canceled a Las Vegas residency over health issues.

“Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever,” the official family statement said. “Dolly was a farmer, just like her Daddy. He farmed the soil; she farmed songs and happiness.”

Parton was known for hit songs such as Jolene and I Will Always Love You, starring in films such as 9 to 5 and Steel Magnolias, and her philanthropy work.

Famous names who knew her or were fans of her work have been paying tribute.

Céline Dion

Céline Dion posted a reminiscence on Instagram:

“We will now be missing one of the most joyful voices this world has ever known. Thank you for the music, the laughter, and the love you gave us all. We will always love you.”

Miley Cyrus

Parton’s goddaughter wrote: “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts.”

She added: “I will always love her and want to make her proud. My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.”

Oprah Winfrey

Winfrey shared a photo of one of her “fondest memories” with Parton, “having a hoot and a holler while wearing Bob Mackie gowns on her show Dolly”. She continued:

“This girl from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee dreamed a life and then lived a life bigger than she could have ever imagined, giving so generously to others in ways we saw and ways we didn’t.

“No one like her. She brought the light, and we are all better because she was here.

God bless you, Dolly – you earned your wings.”

Taylor Swift

In a statement released to press, Swift said:

“A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real or right. But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one.

“Somehow she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person. She possessed the softest heart when it came to the struggles of others, and a backbone of steel to defend her own self-worth as an artist.

“Along with her other fans, I am so grateful for all of it. For the melodies and lyrics she wrote that thawed even the coldest hearts. For the millions of books she provided children all over the world so that they might fall in love with stories the way she did. For the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too. Dolly, I’ll think of you each step of the way.”

Beyoncé

The singer, who collaborated with Parton on a new version of Jolene on her last album, paid tribute in a statement published to her website:

“Dolly, you were the barometer. The north star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship.

“I’m honored that I had the privilege to work with you. I will treasure that forever. Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully.”

Kacey Musgraves

“The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden,” wrote the country star.

Jane Fonda

In a lengthy and emotional Instagram post, Parton’s 9 to 5 co-star wrote: “I know that millions are mourning and I want to say this – more than anyone I have ever known, Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever.” She also added that she was “the voluptuous embodiment of empathy”.

Lily Tomlin

Parton’s 9 to 5 co-star shared a picture of the singer on X, writing: “Friend. Songwriter. The Great Harmonizer of Humanity. Dolly. Dolly. Dolly. Forever Dolly.”

Jamie Lee Curtis

Alongside a photo on Instagram, the Oscar-winning actor wrote: “Thank you, Dolly. For all of it.”

Sabrina Carpenter

The singer remembered Parton as an “angel walking on the earth”.

“I will cherish our laughter and conversations and I will keep your wisdom, your playful outlook on life, and perfect sense of humor in my pocket for the rainy days,” she wrote. “There will never be another you and how lucky are we all to have experienced your singular magic as well as your once in a lifetime voice, songs, and heart.”

Elton John

The singer wrote that he was “shocked and devastated to hear of Dolly’s passing. A giant of an artist – unique and irreplaceable, with the kindest heart.”

Paul McCartney

McCartney, who collaborated with Parton and Ringo Starr on a cover of Let It Be on her 2023 album Rockstar, shared this tribute on Instagram:

“The magnificent star Dolly Parton has died and it is so sad. She was such a wonderful woman. I first met her in Nashville at the Grand Ole Opry where she had been playing with the country star Porter Wagoner and was about to start her solo career. She was so bubbly and full of life it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed.”

“Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music and it is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly. She was a very clever business woman who understood the value of her music and, most importantly, the effect that she had on the people of the world.

“There was no greater honour for me than to have her sing my song Let It Be and, even though I only made a small contribution to it, I am so honoured that she did it. I am so proud to have known her and admire her unique talents.

“Thanks Dolly for the beautiful music you gave me and the whole world. We will always love you, god bless and rest in peace. You were the best.”

Bernie Sanders

In a post on X, the Vermont senator called her “one of the great entertainers of our era” but also “a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief”.

Keith Urban

In an Instagram story, the country star wrote: “Heartbroken today. Honestly … I have no words right now.”

Patti LaBelle

The singer and close friend of Parton said she was “deeply saddened by the loss of my dear friend who was loved by all”.

“Dolly’s artistry, brilliance, and extraordinary life inspired so many people, including me,” LaBelle told CNN. “Her light will forever shine! I send my deepest condolences to all of her loved ones and fans all over the world!”

Julia Roberts

Parton’s Steel Magnolias co-star shared a statement, saying: “Dolly was a magical and joyous human. I hold knowing her as a treasure in my life. The sun has dimmed today.”

Dionne Warwick

Alongside a picture of Parton and herself, the singer posted: “I will certainly miss her laughter, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend. My heart is heavy.”

Barack Obama

The former US president wrote on X: “It’s hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton. Born in a one-room cabin, she earned 11 Grammys and an Emmy, built a business empire, helped millions of kids learn to read, and – as if that wasn’t enough – helped accelerate the research that led to the Moderna Covid vaccine. What a life. Michelle and I are thinking of Dolly’s family and her many, many fans.”

Eminem

The rapper shared a letter Parton sent to him after he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. “Even though I don’t know a lot about rap music, I’ve come to know you are the very best of it,” Parton wrote to him, adding: “I have always felt some unexplained connection to you like I know you somehow … no matter how complex your world may be just know you are very special and touch people in ways you don’t even know.”

“I’m sorry we never got a chance to meet, but getting this note from Dolly really had an impact on me,” Eminem wrote. “She definitely didn’t have to take the time to do it. Even for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon. A superstar in every sense. Rest easy Dolly. And thank you for the kind words.”

Octavia Spencer

The Oscar-winning actor shared a post on Instagram, writing: “Dolly you were a gift to the world, your voice, your philanthropic heart, and warmth made us a feel seen and that the world was a pretty decent place. We miss you.”

Reba McEntire

The country star shared a picture of the pair on Instagram, adding: “Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart.”

Tim Cook

The Apple CEO called Parton “a brilliant songwriter, cultural icon, and dedicated philanthropist” and praised her for helping to “instill a love of reading and learning in millions of children around the world”.

Seth MacFarlane

The actor and animator, who worked with Parton on sci-fi comedy series The Orville, wrote that the experience had been “extraordinary”. “Her kindness, generosity, and authenticity were evident from moment one, and the benign yet assured command she maintained over her empire was obvious from the genuine love and trust you could see from everyone who worked for her,” he posted online. “The world is a dimmer place today without her.”

Bret Michaels

The Poison singer also shared on Facebook: “Sending my deepest thoughts, prayers and condolences on the loss of the incredible Dolly Parton to her close family and friends. Dolly, you have forever added so much to our world and will forever be loved.”

Mick Jagger

The Rolling Stones frontman wrote on X: “What a wonderful songwriter and singer Dolly was. She brought so many people together, we will all miss her so much.”

Belinda Carlisle

The singer-songwriter called Parton “a light in this world” and wrote that she was “heartbroken” by the news.

‘It destroyed me’ – your top true-crime TV shows of all time

The Guardian Wed, 26 Aug 2026 06:57:05 GMT

From influencers gone (really, really) bad and the outrageous Joe Exotic to the greatest reveal in television history – here are Guardian readers’ favourite real-life documentaries and whodunnits

I watched the BBC’s Unsolved: The Boy Who Disappeared when it came out and Damien Nettles, its subject, still pops up in my mind sometimes. It’s a comprehensive, empathetic and gripping investigation into a case I had never heard of. The Serial/Making a Murderer-style approach of showing the investigation, rather than just presenting information, gives the series a much more human angle. I thought it might turn up new evidence; that level of faith in the work being shown is a testament to how thorough it was. AJ, Devon, UK

I remember watching this with my dad. It came on TV late, as part of the Storyville strand, when I was about 20 and working in a pub, living at home. We were captivated by this story about a wrongly accused Black teenager and his trial for allegedly shooting an older white woman. It opened my eyes to police corruption, mistaken identity in lineups and the deep-rooted racism that underlies them. The accused boy is so incredibly normal, like friends of mine at the time, or my younger brother – and the impossibility that he decided to rob and shoot someone on a Sunday morning seems obvious. It is a beautiful piece of sensitive, non-sensationalist film-making with humanity at its heart. Rose, Wakefield, UK

I’m not a fan of true crime TV, but I did see the outrageous Tiger King and found it immensely watchable. Big-cat enthusiast Joe Exotic – who was jailed for animal abuse and two counts of attempted murder for hire, for plotting to kill a rival feline conservationist, Carole Baskin – is the kind of over-the-top character who seems as if he had sprung from a work of fiction. Bruce, Florida, US

To call this a favourite is maybe not the right word; it’s the story of the family vlogger Ruby Franke and the the severe child abuse she committed. The camera footage – the story unfolding before us – made the documentary about this unforgivable crime difficult, albeit engaging, to watch. It’s horrific seeing educated people punishing children in a very cruel way. It helped to know before watching that the two perpetrators were jailed. Judith, Tyne and Wear, UK

This series, which focused on a murder in journalist Mobeen Azhar’s hometown of Huddersfield, was fantastic. Starting with the investigation of a single crime, the story evolves unexpectedly into a really interesting dive into societal and cultural issues, and Azhar’s personal connection to the place means he is clearly invested. It’s one of the best explorations of crime in modern Britain that I’ve seen and it’s available on BBC iPlayer. Neil Marshall, 43, Glasgow, UK

I watched Confessions With a Killer: The Ted Bundy Tapes for the first time with a friend during my first year of uni – and then maybe 100 times since. It’s the high-water mark of an anthology series that also featured Charles Manson and John Wayne Gacy, balancing the sensational and truthful admirably, and giving due respect to the victims. It also allows Bundy to continually dob himself in, emphasising his monstrous ego and lack of empathy. Psychologically and in highlighting the police successes and failures, I still find it fascinating. It’s led to a lifelong fascination with true crime. Issy, 27, London, UK

I saw this about 15 years ago on a Thursday afternoon when I was off sick from work. It destroyed me. My girlfriend (now wife) came home to find me in floods of tears over the amazing David and Kathleen Bagby and how they dealt with the murder of their son, Andrew, and then the murder-suicide of his former partner, Shirley Turner (the main suspect in Andrew’s death), and one-year-old baby son, Zachary. I made everyone watch it, with the caveat that it will make you cry uncontrollably. Even typing this now, it’s making me teary, not least as it was made by Kurt Kuenne – a close friend of Andrew’s. John Fitzgerald, 58, Manchester, UK

The Staircase first appealed to me for its intimate view into a family in crisis. It’s a dramatisation, starring Colin Firth and Toni Collette, of a French documentary that first aired in 2004, about the case of an American novelist accused of murdering his wife (but who he claims fell down the stairs). From there, the rollercoaster progresses – slowly but no less exhilaratingly. The sentiments go from “there are just too many coincidences, he must be guilty”, to “he may be guilty, but the evidence is shoddy at best”, to “even if he is guilty, the American justice system is the real bad guy here and he should never have been convicted”, to ultimately believing that he probably is innocent. As a brother to a criminal defence lawyer, I always prefer true crime that helps unjustly convicted people. The Staircase is a great example of that. Michiel Pauw, 38, Amsterdam, the Netherlands

OJ: Made in America is such a great journey, using the story of OJ Simpson’s life, career and crimes to explain the history of modern civil rights in America. At the end of the series, you feel so captivated by the intertwining themes that you need time to synthesise it all. It’s a well put together series that shows the antecedents to broader societal trends. Anonymous, Australia

This is a Robbery is an in-depth look at the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum heist in Boston in 1990. It remains unsolved and the artwork has never been found. It’s really well done and digs into all the weirdness and oddities that were part of the crime. What makes it especially wild is that Isabella Gardner’s will meant that the paintings couldn’t be replaced – so to this day, the spaces on the wall remain empty. Jose Ramirez, 55, Tewksbury, Massachusetts, US

The Jinx is probably the greatest true crime TV show of the modern era, certainly since Errol Morris’s The Thin Blue Line. Durst – who was suspected of killing his first wife, and was convicted for the murder of a friend and then a neighbour in 2000-01 – is a remarkable subject: a manipulative Jekyll and Hyde-type figure clearly with a great capacity for violence, but charismatic and vulnerable with it, and who is finally undone by his own entitlement and hubris. Watching him ignore the advice of his lawyers and wander inexorably into self-incrimination is highly entertaining. Andrew Jarecki is a fantastic storyteller, and the story itself unfolds with all the twists and turns to keep you completely engrossed. What it demonstrates about what wealth does to people, and how it leverages the legal system, is instructive. Combine all this with the jaw-dropping final reveal and it is about as good as true crime gets! Yvette, Bristol, UK

Unsolved Mysteries is the granddaddy of the true crime TV genre. Robert Stack was the perfect host (when he died in 2003, Dennis Farina took take over hosting duties until the end of its first run), spinning intriguing and sometimes wild and weird mysteries that you wished you could help solve. I’m sure that series helped inspire many of the armchair internet sleuths that popped up in the decades that followed. Robert Graves, 58, Los Angeles, US

The Keepers explores the unsolved murder of Sister Catherine Cesnik in 1969, after she grew to suspect that a priest at the Catholic high school she taught at in Baltimore had sexually abused students. This was the first true crime documentary that caught my attention. I watched and rewatched it several times, perhaps because I lived in the area in Maryland where the case happened. Susan Wilt, New York, US

My favourite crime series has to be American Murder: The Family Next Door on Netflix. The way it’s filmed is equally enthralling and infuriating. The effect of Chris Watts’s attempts to cover up the murder of his pregnant wife and children in the town of Frederick, Colorado, in 2018 is chilling. You feel so much for his late wife, as one horrible man goes on a tear to change his life. Dane Klingaman, 40, Phoenixville, Pennsylvania, US

True crime dramas have become a guilty pleasure in retirement. Like many viewers, I justify the prurient aspect by thinking they might teach us how to avoid similar events and that they honour the victims. Last Stop Larrimah tells the story of the disappearance of an elderly, eccentric Irish immigrant from the tiny Australian outback “town” of Larrimah – population 11, falling to 10. Despite the underlying human tragedy of Paddy Moriarty’s disappearance, I found myself laughing out loud as we meet the inhabitants of Larrimah and hear their stories. As the series progresses and we begin to learn of the tensions between the residents, the tone becomes darker. In the end, this series shines a light on the human condition and Larrimah becomes a microcosm of the wider world. Tim Powell, 67, Worcestershire, UK
